#9586. As People Live Longer, How Can We Live Better?

Become a subscribing member today. Help us continue to bring “the science of a meaningful life” to you and to millions around the globe.

Greater Good Science Center • Magazine • In Action • In Education

When the Stanford Center on Longevity launched in 2007, founding director Laura Carstensen spent a lot of time correcting misperceptions. “The initial response people had was, ‘Like the Methuselah Foundation? You are going to extend life?’” Carstensen was clear that the center’s aim was not to increase lifespans—which had nearly doubled during the 20th century—but rather to build societies that accommodated that new and unprecedented reality.

Another persistent misperception was that “longevity” is a euphemism for aging and that the Stanford Center on Longevity was a center on aging. As Carstensen noted often, “Longevity is not synonymous with aging. It is a metric of length.” The center’s interest is in the challenges and opportunities that longer lives present. While the center is keenly interested in older people, in Carstensen’s view, “longer lives have implications for every stage of life, and the roots of many problems faced at advanced ages have their roots much earlier in life.” The center’s mission is to use longer lives to improve quality of life at all ages.

In 2019, under Carstensen’s leadership, the center launched the New Map of Life initiative, designed to rethink the human life course in response to skyrocketing life expectancies, and it has trained nearly 40 postdoctoral fellows, mentored by faculty affiliates spanning multiple disciplines, about the ways in which longevity is transforming societies, cultures, and economies. After nearly 20 years, Carstensen, the Fairleigh S. Dickinson Jr. Professor in Public Policy and a professor of psychology at Stanford, will step down this summer from her role at the Stanford Center on Longevity to pursue a new project alongside her research and teaching.

I spoke with Carstensen about what she’s learned along the way and what’s next. This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

Karen Breslau: What’s changed since the center’s early days?

Laura Carstensen: I hope it’s clearer that the aging process has not changed much, if any, genetically over the last several thousand years. Rather, longevity—the length of life—increased, and that has enormous implications for nearly all aspects of our lives. The modifiability of aging, on the other hand, is also clear. Even though we’re essentially the same physiological beings that our ancestors were, we changed the world in ways that are allowing us to live healthier and longer. That’s why we are confident that we can build a world where the majority of people live well for a century.

KB: You are on the scientific advisory council to the Health District of Singapore, which is building the Queenstown Health District, a very intentional all-ages community that is incorporating principles from the New Map of Life. What are you seeing?

LC: The Singapore government has given a group of scientists the freedom to design a neighborhood in ways that support long-term health and intergenerational connections, continued financial security, and exercise. They’re thinking about all the factors that contribute to long, healthy, and engaged lives and literally programming them into the community. What’s really cool about the Queenstown Health District is that it can provide a proof of concept that social and physical designs can improve long life.

Already they have built parks and playgrounds with swings for the kids and balance beams for older residents, to provide shared spaces where different ages interact. When we advisers fly in from different countries, we’re starry-eyed at what they can do. Singapore can do things like this in part because they’re smaller, and their government can act quickly. For example, the government recognized about a decade ago that people weren’t saving enough for retirement. So they flipped a switch and said, “OK, everybody’s putting in more money into their retirement account.”

KB: If you had to give a grade to where the U.S. is in implementing the New Map of Life principles, could you take out your red pen?

LC: Compared to some countries, like Singapore, I’d give the U.S. a C-minus, and I am used to grade inflation! The federal government has done little to improve longevity. Unlike the Singapore government, which can require people to save more for retirement, for example, the U.S. cannot quickly implement such programs. On the other hand, in part because the government contributes less, we see a lot of innovation coming from the private sector. We have entire industries offering new products and services. So I’m optimistic about what the U.S. can contribute to longevity. At a global level, it’s fabulous to think about the different approaches that can come from the public and private sectors in a range of countries.

KB: Longevity has gone mainstream and led to billions of dollars in market interest. How has that changed the center’s work?

LC: It’s true that vast investments are going to longevity. Most of these funds are directed at ways that individuals can live longer. There isn’t, in my experience, much philanthropic interest in this space aimed at helping people live better as we live longer lives. I am discouraged that we are sleepwalking through this seismic demographic shift without investing more in the opportunity to rewrite the life scripts that have guided life and imagining ways that we could use them to improve life.

It’s also discouraging that as longevity has entered public consciousness, much of what we hear about are pitches for questionable products that supposedly make people live longer. There are so many snake-oil salesmen in this space that it’s hard for consumers to distinguish what is evidence-based and what is not.

KB: As you often say, transitions are a feature of longer lives. What’s happening next for you?

LC: I’m going to focus more on research and teaching, but first I’m going on sabbatical and look forward to having more time for the things I love—my garden, being at home, sitting in the sun, going for walks. I want to take Pilates lessons. I’m going to take a break in my schedule to say, “How do I create a healthy lifestyle going forward and build the rest around it?”

While I hopefully will have a more relaxed schedule, during my sabbatical I’ll be developing an online course called The Fundamentals of Longevity, which will tell the story of longevity and the potential to live longer, better lives, a change we really need in the world. The course will be accessible far beyond Stanford, so that we can help frame the conversation around longevity and help people appreciate the extraordinary promise of science, technology, and social change to improve life. There is a crisis on the horizon if we don’t change the way we live.

We have the opportunity to change our lives for the better. We have opportunities no previous generation of humans in history has had, and we need to start implementing them.

#9585. UK art market growth lags behind competitors, new report finds

The UK art market has more than tripled in size over the past 30 years but has fallen behind the pace of growth seen by its principal competitors, with mounting regulation identified as one of the key potential barriers to growth.

A report published this week to mark the 30th anniversary of the British Art Market Federation (BAMF), authored by Arts Economics, found that the UK remained the world’s second-largest art market by sales value, growing from £2.6bn in 1996 to £8bn in 2025. The UK also continues to enjoy the dominant position in Europe, with its hold over 50% of the continent’s market share.

However, its recovery from successive economic shocks has been weaker than that of its major competitors. Since the market’s low point in 2009 following the global financial crisis, UK sales have risen by 17% to 2025, compared with 114% growth in the US and 51% globally.

"While celebrating three decades of growth and cultural contribution, our sector faces clear hurdles," says Thomas Christopherson, Chairman of BAMF, in a release accompanying the report, which was launched at a reception at Christie’s in London, on 27 October. "Over-complicated and excessive regulation continues to disproportionately impact the many small and micro businesses that form the backbone of the UK art market. If we are to maintain our competitive edge against major global peers, the heavy burden of compliance must be addressed so that our galleries and auction houses can continue to invest, expand, and thrive."

Given the report’s finding that 89% of UK art businesses reported annual sales below £1 million, the potential burden of regulatory obligations on small teams is evident.

Patterns of cross-border trade are also shifting. UK imports of art and antiques are down 45% from £4.1bn in 2015, to £2.2bn in 2025. UK exports, meanwhile, stand at £3.1bn in 2025, down 48% from £6bn recorded in 2015.

Beyond this contraction, the report notes a diversification of trading partners. In 2000, the United States dominated the UK’s export market, taking 72% of the total value, followed by Switzerland (14%), Japan (2%), and China, Australia and Qatar (1% each). The US remained the largest single destination in 2025, but its share had fallen to 35%, less than half its earlier level. Exports were by then spread across a far broader range of markets, with Switzerland (11%), France (10%) and the Netherlands (6%) among the leading recipients.

There were signs of resilience in the domestic market, however. UK public auction sales rose by 8% to £2.1bn, and the report underlines the sector’s wider economic importance, with the UK art market found to be supporting an estimated 53,290 jobs across 8,780 businesses and generating £1.5bn in tax revenue in 2025. It also underpins the livelihoods of an estimated 62,800 visual artists, according to the report.

Art dealers and auction houses spent an estimated £2bn on ancillary services and products in 2025, equivalent to around a quarter of their turnover.

"Our success is built on a long tradition of specialist skills and expertise in buying and selling art, the benefits of which support thousands of jobs, nurture specialist ancillary businesses, generate tax revenues, and contribute to Britain’s cultural life," said BAMF’s president, Anthony Browne, in the release.

This positive impact is also seemingly reaching beyond the capital. While London remains a major international hub, 65% of employer-registered art businesses are based elsewhere in the UK.

#9584. Holiday anxiety: causes, symptoms, and 10 ways to cope

Clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, CDCES, MBA

We often think of the holiday season as a magical time filled with joy, family gatherings, and celebrations. And it can be. However, for many people, this time of year can also usher in a wave of holiday anxiety, a type of stress associated with the many demands and expectations of the festive season.

Holiday anxiety is a specific type of stress that occurs during holiday seasons. It's different from everyday stress, because it's linked to the unique pressures and expectations that come with holiday events and traditions. Understanding holiday anxiety and recognizing its effects on our mental health can help us manage it effectively. Here are some of the ways it can manifest:

Emotional overload: The holidays can bring a range of emotions, both happy and sad. For some, reminders of lost loved ones or past experiences can lead to feelings of grief or nostalgia.

Physical symptoms: Anxiety can cause physical symptoms like headaches, fatigue, or digestive problems. These can be exacerbated by holiday indulgences and disrupted routines.

Social stress: The pressure to socialize, host events, or interact with family members you might not see regularly can be overwhelming, especially if there are a lot of late nights involved. This is especially true for those with existing social anxieties.

Routine disruption: Regular routines are often disrupted during the holidays, which can be particularly challenging for those who find comfort and stability in their daily schedules.

Acknowledge your feelings around holiday anxiety and remember that it's okay to feel stressed or overwhelmed during the holiday season. Taking proactive steps to manage your mental health can help make the holidays a more enjoyable and less stressful time.

Increased stress levels: Additional demands in the holiday season can lead to heightened stress levels, impacting mental health.

Mood fluctuations: The highs and lows can cause mood swings, bouts of sadness, irritability, and even depression.

Sleep disruption: Anxiety can disturb sleep patterns, leading to insomnia or poor-quality sleep, which, in turn, affects overall wellbeing.

Unhealthy coping mechanisms: Some people might resort to habits like overeating, excessive drinking, or withdrawing from social interactions, which can further impact their mental health.

While what triggers one person may not trigger another, there are a few ways that holiday anxiety can manifest. Identifying your unique triggers can help you prepare tools and strategies to better handle anxiety during this busy season. While the holidays can be an important time, protecting your mental health is more important.

The media and social norms often portray the holidays as a time of perfection and endless joy. This can set unrealistic expectations for the ideal holiday experience, leading to disappointment and stress when reality doesn't match these ideals.

Holidays often come with financial burdens, including the cost of gifts, travel, decorations, and hosting events. Worrying about how to afford these expenses can cause significant stress.

Holidays often feature family gatherings, which can be challenging if relationships are strained or there's a history of conflict. Navigating these dynamics, especially in larger gatherings, can bring anxiety.

The holiday season is filled with invitations to social events, expectations to meet, and tasks to complete. Trying to do everything can lead to burnout and feeling overwhelmed.

For those who’ve lost loved ones or are far from family, the holidays can intensify feelings of grief or isolation. The contrast between personal experience and the general festivity can be overwhelming.

Comparing your own holiday experience to what others seem to be doing online or social media can lead to feelings of inadequacy and dissatisfaction.

Traveling during the holidays can be chaotic and stressful because of busy airports, traffic jams, and the fear of plans being disrupted or not going as scheduled.

The change in daily routines during the holidays, such as altered eating habits, sleep schedules, and exercise, can contribute to stress and anxiety.

Managing holiday anxiety effectively involves practical strategies that focus on self-care and mindfulness. These tips can help you navigate the holiday season with less stress, more enjoyment, and better mental health.

Make a list of holiday activities and rank them in order of importance to you. Focus on the top few that bring you the most joy or are the most meaningful. This can help reduce the feeling of being overwhelmed, ensuring you spend your time and energy on what truly matters to you.

Cut back on elaborate plans. Instead, go for simpler celebrations or low-key gatherings to reduce the pressure and expectations. Smaller, intimate gatherings often bring more joy than large, stressful events.

Enjoy holiday treats but avoid overeating by listening to your body's hunger and fullness cues. Mindful eating can help you maintain physical and mental wellbeing, as overindulgence can often lead to physical discomfort and emotional guilt.

💙 Explore Tamara Levitt’s Mindful Eating Practice and learn the fundamentals of mindfulness at mealtime and how it can help your overall stress and anxiety.

Remind yourself that it’s okay for things not to be perfect, and be realistic about what you can achieve and what the holidays can offer. Having realistic expectations can significantly reduce disappointment and stress.

💙 Learn to let go of what was supposed to be and embrace what is with Jay Shetty’s guided meditation on Expectations.

Don’t pack your schedule too tightly. Instead, plan for breaks and downtime in your holiday schedule. Rest is essential for helping you to recharge, and it allows opportunities for spontaneous activities, too.

💙 When it’s time for bed, make it count by listening to Oren Jay Sofer’s guided sleep meditation, Deep Rest.

Whenever you feel stressed, take a moment to focus on your breathing. Inhale deeply for a count of four, hold for a count of four, and exhale for a count of four to help calm the mind and reduce anxiety.

💙 Use your breath to calm your mind and anxiety in three minutes with Breathe to Calm Down.

Set a budget for holiday spending and stick to it. Consider homemade gifts or shared experiences instead of expensive purchases. This can help reduce holiday anxiety caused by financial strain.

💙 Set Financial Intentions and goals this holiday season, and stick to them.

Not everything will go as planned, so be open to accepting it, and find humor and joy in the imperfect moments. Embracing imperfection can lead to a more relaxed and enjoyable holiday experience.

💙 Shift your energy from perfectionism to going with the flow with this meditation on Energy Management to help guide you toward ease.

Reduce the time you spend on social media to avoid unhealthy comparisons. Limiting social media can help maintain a more realistic perspective and reduce feelings of inadequacy.

💙 Release yourself from the Social Mania comparison by forgoing social media during the holidays.

Reach out to supportive friends, family, or a professional if you feel the holiday stress is too much to handle alone. Talking about your feelings and sharing your experiences can provide relief and remind you you’re not alone in your feelings.

The holidays can be a source of anxiety due to a combination of high expectations, financial pressures, family dynamics, and the disruption of normal routines. The holidays are often portrayed as a time of complete joy and perfect family gatherings, but when reality doesn't match up, it can lead to feelings of inadequacy or disappointment. The holidays can also be a reminder of lost loved ones or past difficulties, contributing to feelings of sadness or loneliness for many people.

The 3-3-3 rule is a simple mindfulness technique to help ground yourself during anxious moments. This exercise can help bring your focus back to the present, interrupting the cycle of anxious thoughts.

Name three things you can see around you.

Move three parts of your body, like your ankle, fingers, and shoulder.

There are plenty of actionable ways to calm holiday anxiety.

Prioritize self-care activities like mindful breathing or a relaxing bath.

Engage in regular physical activity to help relieve stress.

Keep a regular sleep schedule to ensure adequate rest.

Set realistic expectations for the holidays.

Simplify plans and focus only on what matters most to you.

Seek support from friends, family, or professionals.

It's completely normal to feel overwhelmed during Christmas. The holiday season can be a hectic time with lots of social obligations, financial pressures, and the emotional weight of personal or family expectations. It's important to recognize these feelings and take steps to manage them, like setting boundaries, asking for help when needed, and taking time for self-care.

To manage social anxiety during Thanksgiving, plan ahead for social interactions. Have some conversation topics ready to ease into interactions. Set boundaries for yourself, and step away for a moment if you feel overwhelmed. Focus on making connections with one or two people rather than trying to engage with everyone. Practice relaxation techniques such as deep breathing before and during the event. And remember, it's okay to limit social gatherings to what feels manageable for you.

Yes. Anxiety can build before a trip, show up during it, or both, often from planning pressure or the work you left behind. If this is your main concern, our guide to vacation anxiety covers what to do before, during, and after your holiday.

#9583. When Your Loved Ones Are Your Child’s Biggest Critic

ADDitude readers share the hurtful ways family and friends treat their neurodivergent children, from spewing ignorant comments to purposefully excluding them, and how they combat them.

ADHD understanding has improved in recent decades, but many people still just don’t get it – and sometimes those people are the ones closest to us.

Hearing your child criticized or misjudged hurts. Hearing criticisms and barbs from family members and friends who don’t understand ADHD ushers in a complicated whirlwind of emotions. You may feel like an inadequate parent. You may worry whether your child will be accepted at family get-togethers. You may grow weary of explaining your child’s condition.

If this is you, you’re not alone. More than 73% of ADDitude readers say they have relatives or friends who criticize or dislike their neurodivergent child. Read about their experiences and how they navigate them below.

“The older generations are close-minded or under-educated about ADHD and make it seem like it’s made up or an excuse. They say, ‘Everyone says they have ADHD’ or ‘You need to be a better parent.’ I am mostly there to protect my children and correct the person who says it, so my kids don’t feel they are less than.” – Gina, California

“I had a friend who would sugar up my kids intentionally to ‘prove’ that I was over-reacting about the negative side effects of sugar. When the kids misbehaved, she blamed it on my ‘inconsistent parenting’ and not the ADHD brain on sugar and food-coloring!” – An ADDitude Reader

[Get This Free Download: 13 Parenting Strategies for Kids with ADHD]

“We’ve had to deal with side remarks at times from relatives and friends. One example would be someone making retorts to their child like ‘Hey, what are you doing? Even John Doe (my son) would behave better than you right now.’ It’s using my son’s negative behaviors as a frame of reference that my wife and I don’t find helpful at all.” – Jono, Canada

“When my daughter was younger, I was still learning how to handle her behavior, but having family and others say that she was out of control, and that I let her get away with behaviors, really hurt. It made me feel like a bad parent. It took years of working with therapists for me to understand that her behavior and diagnosis were not my fault.” – Deneise, West Virginia

“They just don’t seem to understand that ADHD behaviors aren’t always choices. The only solution seems to be limiting time with the people who don’t understand. Plus, now that the kids are older. I explain to them that some people don’t understand.” – Jenny, Virginia

“My sister-in-law criticizes the amount of ‘stuff’ my children have and their ongoing projects. She doesn’t understand that ADHD brains organize differently and create on a whim, or that having the freedom to be creative is where they excel. I usually head off these comments by talking up their creativity and explaining that they are just brilliantly wired differently.” – An ADDitude Reader, Kansas

“My grandparents and siblings definitely thought we were failing at parenting for a while, and a few friends thought I was a bad mom. Most comments centered on not having strict enough rules/seeing my children’s behavior as bad or rude choices vs. dysregulated behaviors. My village now is almost entirely made up of parents of neurodivergent kids, and we’re all so supportive and understanding of how hard everyone works to provide support and education for our children.” – Acadia, Virginia

“My parents say my child is just lazy in school, and he needs to put more effort into everything. So sometimes I just stop telling them the details. For example, in addition to ADHD, my son recently got diagnosed with dyslexia. I won’t tell them. It’s unfortunate, because he is their grandson and they should know, but I just don’t want to discuss it anymore.” – An ADDitude Reader

“I remind them that they have never parented a child with ADHD, so they do not know what it is like to walk in my shoes. I have also sent them articles about ADHD.” – Sarah, Indiana

“Our dearest friends of 20+ years stopped inviting us to their home for Thanksgiving after a particularly difficult time in their home with our children… The best I have been able to engage with them about this is to ask how their nephew who lives in a different city and is also neurodivergent is doing. When they share difficult times in his regard, I focus the discussion on the antecedents to the disruptive behaviors and try to engage them in problem-solving sleuthing. I connect the conversation with my own experience and invite them to do the same. I have had some deep and meaningful conversations with them over the years, but we still are no longer invited to their home.” – Robyn, North Carolina

“I eventually just cut my family off from contact. The pain they caused my kids was not worth maintaining those relationships.” – Christina, Arizona

#9582. 7 types of anxiety disorders (and how to deal with each one)

Clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, MBA

Your heart starts racing the moment you walk into a crowded room. Even when nothing’s wrong, worry looms in the back of your mind. The thought of a specific fear, like snakes or needles, makes you feel sick. If any of that sounds familiar, anxiety might be part of the picture.

Anxiety doesn't look the same for everyone, which is sometimes why it can be so hard to name. The term "anxiety" covers several disorders, each with its own signs and triggers — though they often overlap, both in how they show up and in what helps.

Anxiety disorders affect roughly 1 in 5 U.S. adults every year. The good news is, they’re typically quite treatable. Let’s break down the seven main types of anxiety listed in the DSM-5 (the manual used for clinical diagnosis), and how to find some relief.

The seven anxiety disorders below share a general thread: they’re rooted in fear or worry that sticks around and gets in the way of daily life. They’re also the most common types, though a few related conditions are worth knowing too (covered further down).

GAD is a persistent, hard-to-control worry that spans multiple areas of your life and shows up more days than not for at least six months. Everyday stress usually has a clear cause and fades once the situation resolves. By contrast, generalized anxiety moves from topic to topic and rarely lets up, because your mind treats any uncertainty as a threat.

This disorder often comes with physical and mental symptoms such as restlessness, muscle tension, fatigue, trouble concentrating, irritability, and disrupted sleep.

What helps: Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is widely used for GAD. It helps you spot and shift the thought patterns that fuel your worries. A regular mindfulness practice can also ease tension by training your attention to stay in the present instead of running through what-ifs.

💙 Start with Calm’s Tools for Stress and Anxiety series.

For a more detailed overview, check out our GAD guide.

A panic attack is a sudden rush of intense fear that brings on physical symptoms—racing heart, tight chest, dizziness—and usually peaks within minutes. A single panic attack doesn't mean you have panic disorder — plenty of people experience one and never have another.

Panic disorder is defined by what comes after the attack, such as ongoing dread about when the next one might hit and routine changes made to avoid triggering one.

This fear response tends to feed itself in a cycle. A normal body signal, like a fast heartbeat, gets misread as danger. That triggers more fear, which leads to more physical symptoms.

What helps: CBT can help you learn to read these body signals as harmless rather than dangerous. It’s often paired with interoceptive exposure, where you deliberately bring on mild versions of those same sensations until they stop feeling threatening. During this process, slow breathing can signal safety to your nervous system.

Discover 5 mindfulness tools to calm you down during a panic attack.

Social anxiety disorder is a strong fear that you’ll be negatively perceived in social or performance situations, often severe enough that dread sets in days before the event itself.

It's much more than being shy. At its core is a belief that you'll do something embarrassing and be judged for it. That belief may lead you to avoid those situations altogether, which can bring short-term relief but reinforces the fear over time.

What helps: Exposure-based CBT has the strongest evidence. It gradually builds your comfort in the situations you've been avoiding by facing them in small, manageable steps. Self-compassion can also make a real difference. Since social anxiety tends to run on harsh self-judgment, practicing kindness toward yourself can help quiet that inner critic.

Not sure if you have social anxiety? Here are signs to look out for.

A specific phobia is a fear of one particular thing—like heights, flying, needles, dogs, or tight spaces—out of proportion to the actual danger. A fear becomes a phobia when it impacts your behavior, whether that’s rerouting a drive to avoid a bridge or skipping a checkup because of needles. Even thinking about the trigger can set off anxiety, so avoiding it becomes your default.

Phobias often start with a scary experience or a fear picked up early in life. Avoidance keeps the fear alive, since your brain never learns that the trigger is safe.

What helps: Exposure therapy is the leading treatment, shown to outperform placebo and other therapies. Pair each step with grounding and breathing techniques to make the process feel more manageable.

Explore the most common phobias and how to deal with them.

Agoraphobia is a fear of being somewhere you couldn't easily escape or get help if panic or embarrassing symptoms hit. This can include public transit, open spaces, crowds, lines, or long stretches away from home alone. Many people with agoraphobia avoid those places altogether.

The DSM-5 classifies it as its own diagnosis. Left untreated, this avoidance can shrink your world, sometimes making it hard to leave the house at all.

What helps: CBT with step-by-step exposure is the first-line treatment, and it helps you return to avoided places gradually. Since agoraphobia and panic often overlap, treatment usually addresses both. To build confidence, try calming techniques at home first, then in triggering places.

Learn 8 evidence-backed ways to manage agoraphobia.

Separation anxiety disorder is an excessive fear about being away from people you're close to. Once seen as a childhood condition, it’s now known to affect adults too. It can show up as real distress when a partner travels or constant worry that something bad will happen to a loved one.

Underneath it is a fear of loss: of the person or of your own ability to cope without them. You may find yourself seeking reassurance or checking in repeatedly, but these responses tend to feed the anxiety rather than calm it.

What helps: CBT can help you reduce your need for reassurance and build comfort with time apart. Mindfulness encourages you to pause when an anxious thought arises and let the worry pass. For severe cases, a doctor may suggest therapy alongside medication.

💙 Practice riding out anxious thoughts with Calm’s Letting Go of Anxiety course.

Selective mutism is an inability to speak in certain social settings where talking is expected, like school or work. It's rare, affecting under 2% of people, and it usually shows up in childhood, though it can last into later years.

This isn't stubbornness or a speech problem — it's fear. You may want to speak, but hold back because of it in those environments.

What helps: Behavioral therapy that slowly builds up speaking in those settings, often involving family or school staff, is the main approach. Early intervention tends to lead to better outcomes, so it’s worth seeking professional guidance as soon as symptoms appear.

While the disorders above are what most people mean by "anxiety," a few related conditions are helpful to understand for the full picture.

Two more fall under the DSM-5's anxiety chapter:

Substance or medication-induced anxiety disorder: This anxiety is caused directly by a substance, whether that’s too much caffeine, a prescription drug, or withdrawal from alcohol. It can be overlooked, which is why a doctor will often ask what you're taking before making a diagnosis.

Anxiety disorder due to another medical condition: A physical illness—such as an overactive thyroid or a heart or lung problem—can cause anxiety. A checkup can rule out this possibility early on, and treating the underlying illness often eases the anxiety too.

Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) and post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) get grouped with anxiety disorders a lot, as they also involve overwhelming fear and distress. But the DSM-5 classifies them separately: OCD centers on unwanted thoughts and behaviors, while PTSD comes after a traumatic event.

If either sounds closer to what you're dealing with, our OCD guide or our complex PTSD guide is a good place to start.

Generalized anxiety disorder (GAD) and panic disorder differ mainly in how the worry builds and shows up. GAD involves a slow-burning worry about many areas of life that rarely fades. Panic disorder centers on sudden, intense attacks and the fear of having another one. It’s possible to have both, and cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) works well for either.

Curious about CBT for anxiety? Here are 5 techniques to try.

The difference between having social anxiety and being introverted comes down to preference versus fear. Introversion is a preference about how you recharge — social time drains your energy, but it doesn't fill you with dread. Social anxiety, meanwhile, brings a fear of judgment or embarrassment, often strong enough to make you skip things you'd enjoy.

It’s not unusual to have more than one anxiety disorder at the same time, and they can show up alongside other conditions including depression. A doctor can help you sort out which ones you’re dealing with, and treatments like CBT can target several disorders at once.

A specific phobia and agoraphobia differ in what the fear is tied to. A specific phobia is about one clear trigger, such as spiders or flying. Agoraphobia is broader: it's a fear of being somewhere you couldn't easily escape or get help, like a crowd or public transit.

The most common types of anxiety in adults are specific phobias, social anxiety disorder, and generalized anxiety disorder. Altogether, anxiety disorders affect close to 1 in 5 U.S. adults each year and are the most prevalent type of mental health condition.

Anxiety disorders can ease on their own for some people, but many stick around or return without treatment. Fortunately, treatment can meaningfully improve your quality of life. Most people find that therapy, medication, or a combination makes a noticeable difference.

The most well-supported therapy for anxiety disorders is cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), often paired with gradual exposure work. Medication is another option with strong evidence, either used alone or alongside therapy. The right fit depends on your specific disorder and its severity, so it's important to consult a professional.

There are several natural ways to manage anxiety, though they aren’t a replacement for clinical treatment. Regular exercise, quality sleep, and cutting back on caffeine and alcohol can all help alleviate how anxious you feel day to day. Mindfulness practices (like breathing exercises or grounding techniques) are especially well-supported, since they teach you to notice anxious thoughts or sensations without getting swept up in them.

#9581. Five Things Students Taught Us About Connecting Across Differences

Become a subscribing member today. Help us continue to bring “the science of a meaningful life” to you and to millions around the globe.

Greater Good Science Center • Magazine • In Action • In Education

When I’m producing a documentary, one of my favorite parts of the process is the moment when a bit of our footage sticks to me. Permanently. I never know when it will happen, but it always does. The sticky bit could be a snippet of dialogue or a quote from an interview. After watching the footage over and over again, the bit becomes part of me.

Often it’s a funny line—a perfect, punchy distillation of the truth that gets adopted as an inside joke among the team of producers and editors. We repeat it like a collective spell that buoys us when we’re sinking under the weight of the project’s heavy subject matter. Sometimes the thing that sticks is not funny at all. Sometimes it’s a splinter, a cutting insight that I would have rather avoided. Or it’s a solidly true, heartfelt moment that sits like a smooth stone in my pocket. The touchstone grounds and guides me on the long journey of making a film.

For the better part of the past year, I’ve been working as an executive producer on a series of short documentaries for the Greater Good Science Center called Connecting on Campus: Stories of Courage, Curiosity, and Empathy. The series features students at four universities across the country who are attempting to connect in some meaningful way with people who have different life experiences, political beliefs, or visions for the future.

At Iliff School of Theology, master’s and Ph.D. students imagine a version of the United States that embodies their values, and then they share those visions with one another. As they listen to one another’s values, they discover where they align, where they diverge, and where empathy can keep them in relationship with each other even when they disagree.

In a two-part story set at Bowie State University and the University of Maryland, students from both campuses gather at an event hosted by the schools’ Social Justice Alliance, a first-of-its-kind collaboration between an HBCU (historically Black college or university) and a PWI (predominantly white institution).

At Dickinson College, a deep friendship between the presidents of the Dickinson College Republicans and the Dickinson College Democrats creates the conditions for an unexpectedly collaborative relationship between the two clubs. Members of both clubs gather regularly and listen to each other’s thoughts about complex and often contentious political issues.

Back when we were in the middle of editing these episodes with our collaborators at Anaconda Street Productions, I spent an afternoon reviewing footage from one of the shoots, and then I took my dog for a walk. On the walk, I found myself repeating a line from an interview. It stuck! It’s been one of those smooth stones in my pocket ever since.

Of course, I’m not the only one who was changed by the experience of working on this series. To celebrate the release of Connecting on Campus, I invite you behind the scenes to meet my collaborators as we share some of the many things we learned as we helped tell these stories.

It’s a pretty straightforward message, yet I hear it over and over in my head in the voice of Mrs. Dawn Collins. Your voice matters and everyone has a part to play. Mrs. Collins says these words during an interview in the first of our two episodes about Bowie State University (BSU) and the University of Maryland (UMD). Mrs. Collins and her husband, Mr. Richard Collins Jr., founded the BSU–UMD Social Justice Alliance after their son, Lt. Richard Collins III, a BSU student, was murdered on the UMD campus by a student in 2017. The Alliance brings together faculty, staff, and students to join the Collins’s commitment to “eradicating the ideology of intolerance, while confronting individuals and combatting systems that normalize indifference, justify injustice, perpetuate hate, and inflict violence.”

Mrs. Collins’s words have stuck with me, in part, because they insist on every person’s dignity, power, and responsibility. Our voices matter, and we all have a role to play in eradicating the ideology of intolerance and in combatting systems that perpetuate hate and inflict violence. That’s a strong call to action.

Mrs. Collins’s words have also stuck with me because they clearly articulate the heart of this documentary series. The students featured in this series offer us examples of what happens when people step into their power and accept the responsibility to understand themselves, understand each other (differences and all), and work together to build something new. That new thing could be a collaboration between clubs on campus or a vision for our future as a nation. Either way, these students know their voices matter and they have what it takes to practice doing this work together.

It was so helpful to have Mrs. Collins’s voice in my head, keeping me anchored in this truth as I worked. — Kelly Rafferty

When we first imagined Connecting on Campus, we wanted to find places where students were actually practicing the skills and qualities that make connection across differences possible, and to make those moments visible.

As I spent time with these students and their stories, and as we shaped the episodes in the edit, I found myself thinking more and more about choice. Across the series, you see students staying curious when they could shut down, listening to understand someone else’s experience, sharing their own perspective while making space for someone else’s, or finding the courage to remain in a difficult conversation.

In our Dickinson College episode, that choice shows up in a moment that could have easily passed. Ryan Thies recounts meeting Matthew Craig at a Halloween party during his freshman year. Matthew was dressed as Donald Trump. Ryan could have seen that costume, made an assumption about who Matthew was, and walked away. Instead, he leaned in and got to know him. An unlikely connection became a friendship, and eventually the two chose to become roommates.    Ryan’s choice changed what became possible between them. That choice reflects the kind of empathy we talk about in our Bridging Differences work: the deliberate, and often difficult, choice to engage with someone else’s experience even when it feels unfamiliar or challenges our own worldview.

The choices look different in our Bowie State University and University of Maryland episodes—and the stakes are obviously very different, too. Here, the students and the Collins family are stepping into a history that is devastating: the murder of Lt. Richard Collins III on the University of Maryland campus and the work that emerged from it to confront hatred and bring students from the two campuses together.

Here, courage looks like choosing to show up and engage when discomfort, conflict, and fear might make it easier—and completely understandable—to withdraw. It’s the decision to say: This matters. I’ll attend. I’ll represent. I’ll listen. I’ll do my part.

Practices like “Listen with Empathy,” “Understand Their Values,” “Expand Your Views and Circles,” or “Perspective Giving and Getting” from our Bridging Differences in Higher Education Playbook can be learned.

But the choice to engage is one each of us has to make. My hope is that people watch these stories asking themselves, “What did that person do that made greater understanding possible, and where might I try that myself?”  — Juliana Tafur

I came away thinking that “bridging” is sometimes misunderstood as compromise. Across all four videos, something more interesting emerges: You can build a relationship across a difference without necessarily resolving the difference itself.

At Iliff School of Theology, students imagine very different versions of America without being asked to arrive at one shared vision. At Dickinson, Republicans and Democrats engage seriously with each other without abandoning their political beliefs. And at Bowie State University and the University of Maryland, students move beyond assumptions, allow themselves to be vulnerable, ask difficult questions, and really listen to people whose backgrounds and experiences differ from their own. The circumstances are very different, but the lesson is consistent: Bridging isn’t about erasing what separates us. It’s about developing the curiosity, trust, and courage to stay connected across those differences.

The series asks a harder and more useful question than “How do we get everyone to agree?” It asks how we live, learn, and build community with people who may never see the world exactly as we do. The answers aren’t presented as a formula. You get to watch people experiment with listening, vulnerability, curiosity, disagreement, and repair, then decide for yourself what actually works. — Omar Lugones

In my own experiences in smaller, more intimate classroom settings, I often observe an echo-chamber effect when opinions are shared, especially when the class is discussing a controversial topic. I have noticed a general apprehension about “going first” or initiating the conversation. Speaking for myself, I am often afraid of offering the “wrong” opinion, meaning a perspective that could be interpreted as supporting a politically or socially unacceptable position and cause my peers to view me as an outsider. I do not necessarily think my peers are experiencing the exact same thought process, but I sense that they are also self-conscious about expressing a conflicting opinion. As a result, people may default to agreeing with whoever offers an opinion first.

I thought it was remarkable that at Iliff School of Theology, Lindsay Ambler and Stephanie Nelson initially disagree with one another, and that moment opens space for others to enter the conversation and offer their own perspectives. By disagreeing respectfully, they demonstrate how disagreement can produce a deeper understanding of an issue than a conversation built only around agreement.

Lindsay takes a strong position on the effects of religion based on her past experiences with Christian institutions. By sharing an extremely vulnerable personal story, she creates the conditions for others to share their experiences and, in turn, promotes a greater sense of empathy within the conversation.

When Stephanie offers her own perspective on whether society can reach a state of perfection and equality, her response conflicts with Lindsay’s position. This point of contention could seemingly disrupt the vulnerable environment Lindsay has created, yet it does not. Instead, Lindsay responds to the challenge by deepening her explanation. In doing so, she creates new points of entry for others to join the conversation and contribute their own experiences.

At the end of the discussion, Stephanie expresses gratitude to those who shared their perspectives and revealed gaps in her own thinking. The conversation demonstrates how respectful disagreement can foster empathy, growth, and greater participation from every member of a group. — Tyler C. Tang

Working on this series, I noticed the relationship between character and discomfort. Courage, empathy, humility, and curiosity all sound admirable in the abstract, but you really discover whether you possess them when another person challenges you. Character in these films often reveals itself in what someone does immediately after hearing something they don’t agree with.

For example, I identified with Josh Perez, a Ph.D. student and teaching assistant at Iliff School of Theology, in particular. I appreciate the way he draws on his own experiences as a second-generation Mexican American while recognizing that other people carry struggles he may never experience himself. His vision isn’t simply about creating a world that works better for people like him. It’s about making room for others to find liberation from their own struggles, as well. That ability to be grounded in your own experience while still making space for the experiences of others is at the heart of bridging differences. — Antonio Carrasco III

If you’re exhausted by watching people argue about politics, identity, and social issues, watch people actually talk to each other instead. The series doesn’t suggest that differences disappear when people sit down together. It shows that disagreement can be productive when people approach each other with curiosity and humility.

Iliff School of Theology student Lindsay Ambler’s story affected me in a way I didn’t expect. It was hard to hear how painful some of her experiences within religious spaces had been. Learning how she was rejected after people discovered she was gay gave me a much deeper understanding of what she carried into the classroom. It reminded me how little we may know about someone until we give them the space to share their story.

Logan Midler from the University of Maryland stands out to me, too. I appreciate how honest she is about not having much interaction with people from different backgrounds and how easy it can be to start those conversations. Her desire to listen, learn, and become a better ally feels like a simple yet powerful example of bridging differences. — Ryan Carrasco

I hope there’s a moment in Connecting on Campus that sticks with you, too. Maybe that memorable line, that bit of dialogue, or that mindful pause will become a touchstone for your own experiments in bridging differences.

As another academic year begins, may the stories in this series also serve as an example of what students are capable of doing when they’re given the space and support to practice connecting with one another. Campuses across the country are facing real challenges—everything from threats of censorship to rising costs and cuts to funding—and these opportunities to practice bridging differences must not be sacrificed along the way. They’re too important to our individual and collective well-being.

Watch Connecting on Campus: Stories of Courage, Curiosity, and Empathy.

#9580. Early Puberty More Common in Girls with ADHD

Neurodivergent girls are more likely to experience early puberty and may be especially vulnerable to its effects. Here, understand why.

Puberty is not a single event, but a years-long process that is both universal and highly individual. It shapes brain and emotional development, identity, and lifelong physical and mental health. If it begins before a child is developmentally ready, it can increase the risk for physical and mental health problems.

Research suggests that girls with ADHD are more likely to enter puberty early and to experience the transition more intensely, placing them at heightened risk for anxiety, depression, eating disorders, and other challenges. Parental guidance, emotional regulation skills, and professional support can buffer these risks by bolstering self-confidence in girls as they navigate the pubertal transition.

Researchers are examining why girls with ADHD have about twice the risk for early puberty, and why autistic girls are up to four times more likely to experience early puberty compared to other children.1 In addition to higher rates of obesity and social stress, which could accelerate the onset of puberty, neurodivergent girls may experience differences in dopamine activity, stress response, and immune and neuroendocrine systems — all of which may affect sexual development.

Early relative puberty — development that begins earlier than average but remains within the typical age range — is different from precocious puberty. In girls, precocious puberty refers to physical and hormonal changes before age 8, including breast and pubic hair development, rapid growth, and menstruation. It requires medical evaluation and treatment. Left unmanaged, it can contribute to shorter adult height, psychosocial distress, and other complications. Two forms exist:

When estrogen and progesterone rise in girls, ADHD symptoms fluctuate. Here’s how:

Rising hormone levels affect the physiological and neural systems involved in emotional processing and regulation.

Girls who menstruate may also experience pronounced changes in ADHD symptoms across the menstrual cycle.

Girls who mature early may feel distressed when their physical development outpaces their cognitive, emotional, and social development.

#9579. How to define cheating in a relationship (and what to do about it)

Clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, MBA

Late-night texts lighting up their phone. A “friend from work” who comes up a little too often when they talk about their day. Or maybe it’s the other way around, and it’s a name you've conveniently left out of your story. Either way, it leads to a quiet, nagging sense that something's off.

Some cheating is obvious. But the old idea that it only counts if it's physical doesn't hold up to how people experience betrayal today. Emotional connections can form through a screen, and it isn't always a single, clear-cut act.

Here’s the big picture on what cheating really means, and what to do if you’re facing it in your own relationship.

Cheating means acting in a way that violates the boundaries and trust that a couple has built together.

The issue is that the boundaries aren’t always clear. Many couples never discuss what's off limits, whether that’s a text to an ex, a close emotional friendship, or a flirtatious dinner. You and your partner may share the same values, and assume you’re aligned on the specifics. Then a moment reveals you’re not.

Where people draw the line on cheating usually traces back to a few underlying factors.

Attachment style: People prone to relationship anxiety may read more behaviors as threatening. People who lean more avoidant may downplay concerning behavior as trivial, including their own.

Cultural and religious background: Some cultures and religions view certain dating norms, like close friendships outside the relationship, as completely normal, while others see them as concerning.

Relationship structure: Couples set their own rules for the relationship, whether that’s monogamy, non-monogamy, or somewhere in between. Those rules define what counts as betrayal.

Related read: How to find your attachment style and deepen your relationships

Infidelity takes many forms, and even within each form, it can look drastically different depending on the situation. Here’s how it tends to show up.

This is the one most people picture first: romantic or sexual contact with someone outside the relationship, without your partner knowing or agreeing to it. That last part is key.

Couples in open relationships can have very different lines. As long as both partners are on the same page, physical intimacy with others can be a normal part of the relationship.

Emotional cheating means forming a close bond with someone outside your relationship that pulls closeness or energy away from your partner.

The line between a close friendship and an emotional affair can feel blurry, but research points to three signs:

Details get shared that don't get shared with your partner.

An unspoken attraction exists, even if neither person names it.

Emotional cheating can be dismissed because nothing physical happened, but many people find it just as painful as physical infidelity, sometimes more so. It tends to build slowly, until the loyalty has quietly shifted.

Virtual cheating is physical or emotional cheating through a screen. This can look like sexting, intimate messaging, or building a close connection online. Some therapists also include excessive pornography use when it's hidden and gets in the way of intimacy with a partner, though opinions vary.

This type of cheating is more accessible than most other forms of infidelity, and is often harder to catch. A message is one tap away, at any hour, with virtually anyone.

Micro-cheating involves smaller, ambiguous behaviors that fall short of the categories above, but can still chip away at trust. Some common examples include:

Keeping a dating profile active "just in case"

Finding constant reasons to message one specific person

Spending time with someone without mentioning it to your partner

Flirting with someone in a way you wouldn't if your partner were present

It comes down to whether it's a repeated pattern your partner wouldn't be okay with.

Financial infidelity means hiding money, concealing debt, keeping secret accounts, or making big financial decisions without telling your partner. It's a serious trust issue, especially in long-term relationships where finances are shared.

This is more common than most people expect and can do just as much damage as other forms of infidelity.

If you’re suspicious of your partner, sitting with that uncertainty can feel unbearable. But before you act on a hunch, try slowing down and approaching the situation with as much calm as you can.

Start by noticing what’s actually happening—and what’s actually changed—versus what you suspect. Has your partner’s communication, availability, or emotional presence shifted in a specific way? Or is this more of a gut sense that something's off?

Both are valid, but knowing which one you’re dealing with can help you decide how to proceed.

💙 Explore Sensations vs. Emotions with Jay Shetty on Calm.

Your unease may not be about your suspicions. It might be disconnection, feeling unappreciated, or a sense that something’s changed between you. Getting clear on what’s bugging you before you bring it up can make the conversation more productive.

💙 Dig deeper with Investigating Anxiety from the Emotions Series on Calm.

You may think that checking their phone, socials, or location data will settle your suspicion about the situation. But it tends to worsen your anxiety.

If you find something, you’re left dealing with what you found and the fact that you went looking. If you don’t, the relief rarely lasts, because whatever made you suspicious in the first place is still unresolved.

A few minutes of focused breathing before a hard conversation can settle your body and quiet your mind. That short reset can help you feel steadier and lead to a clearer conversation for both of you.

💙 Take a Pause to Breathe on the Calm app.

Before you bring something up, think about what you’re hoping for. Do you want clarity? Reassurance? That goal can keep you focused, even if the conversation gets derailed.

Approaching the discussion with an open mind, rather than jumping to accusations, often invites a more honest exchange.

Instead of starting with “I think you’re cheating on me,” try something along the lines of “I’ve been feeling disconnected and I’d like to talk about it.”

Whether you're dealing with confirmed infidelity or unresolved suspicion, you don't have to process it alone. Support from a therapist, individually or as a couple, can offer a structured space to work through it.

Sometimes suspicion itself, even without proof of cheating, may be a sign that the relationship needs attention.

Cheating is a violation of the spoken or unspoken agreements you and your partner have made about exclusivity. It can show up physically, emotionally, or virtually, and what counts can look different from couple to couple. Secrecy and broken trust are usually the common thread.

Read more: Here's how to work through the most common relationship issues

The main types of cheating are physical, emotional, and virtual, though subtler patterns such as financial secrecy or "micro-cheating" can apply too.

Physical cheating involves intimate contact outside the relationship. Emotional cheating involves a close bond kept hidden from your partner. Virtual cheating involves a romantic connection through a screen.

Emotional cheating can feel just as harmful as physical cheating, and for some people, more so. It often builds slowly, through shared thoughts and private moments your partner doesn't know about.

Physical cheating usually involves specific, identifiable moments, while emotional cheating often unfolds gradually, as loyalty fades over time.

Cheating almost always involves some kind of concealment. Being vague, withholding details, or keeping a connection secret are all forms of it. Sometimes it's the hiding, more than the act itself, that turns it into a betrayal.

Couples can define cheating differently, based on their values, culture, and the specific agreements they've made. Partners in open relationships, for example, may knowingly allow behaviors that other couples wouldn't. What’s important is that you and your partner are on the same page about boundaries.

Disagreements over what’s considered cheating are worth addressing head-on. A transparent conversation about your expectations and boundaries can feel uncomfortable, but it's one of the more protective things you can do for a relationship. A couples therapist can support this conversation if it feels overwhelming to navigate alone.

When you’re talking to your partner about what’s bothering you, try focusing on your own experience rather than their behavior. Something like "I've been feeling distant and want to check in with us" opens the door for an honest conversation instead of a defensive one.

In some cases, trust can be rebuilt after cheating, though it takes consistent effort from both of you. Many couples find professional support helpful along the way.

It usually requires transparency and accountability to understand what led to the breach. Leaving is a valid choice too, as long as the decision is made carefully.

Read more: Recovering from infidelity: 6 tips to help couples heal from an affair

#9577. ‘Encounter the unexpected’: Harry Houdini exhibition commemorates the famed illusionist on the centenary of his death

Unidentified photographer, Houdini in his home office, around 1925 Courtesy of the Ken Trombly Collection

The famed escape artist Harry Houdini dreamed of retiring to his library and spending the rest of his life writing about the many topics that filled its volumes: the history of conjuring, witchcraft, psychic phenomena and the drama of the stage.

“Every hour which I could spare from my professional work was given over to study in libraries, to interviews with retired magicians and collectors, and to browsing in old bookstores and antique shops where rare collections of programmes, newspapers and prints might be found,” he wrote in his 1908 book The Unmasking of Robert-Houdin. In the townhouse he shared with his wife, Bess, at 278 West 113th Street in Manhattan, ephemera and books were crammed into shelves and stacked in precarious piles.

Unidentified photographer, Harry Houdini in a publicity photo for his silent film The Grim Game, 1919. Harry Houdini Papers, Harry Ransom Center, The University of Texas at Austin.

On 31 October 1926, he died suddenly while on tour at the age of 52 from a ruptured appendix. The thousands of items he had devoted years to amassing were dispersed, with his magic collection going to the Library of Congress. The drama collection, after passing through a series of hands, arrived at the University of Texas at Austin in 1958, where it is held by the Harry Ransom Center.

“There was a misconception, even within the magic community, that what came to the Ransom Center was just an incredible collection of Houdini’s personal papers, not realising that there’s material on magic dating back hundreds of years that doesn’t exist anywhere else, and that had all come from Houdini, too,” says Eric Colleary, the centre’s curator of theatre and performing arts.

Installation view of Houdini's Library at the Harry Ransom Center Photo: Trent Lesikar

After he joined the Ransom Center in 2015, Colleary started noticing traces of Houdini’s collection everywhere, whether engravings of mechanical automata or theatrical playbills dating back to the 18th century that most others at the time treated as disposable. “He mentioned it in almost every interview he gave,” Colleary says. “He figured out ways to work it into letters that had nothing to do with his collection. It was really important to him.”

Colleary has now spent over a decade unravelling the depth of Houdini’s bibliophilia, an effort that has culminated in the Houdini’s Library exhibition at the Ransom Center (until 24 January 2027) and a book of the same name out now from Abbeville Press. The curator’s detective work to illuminate this lesser-known side of the legendary magician included tracking down a lost mahogany bookcase that had held his theatrical materials and examining Houdini’s typescript catalogue that is now at David Copperfield’s International Museum and Library of the Conjuring Arts in Las Vegas. The 53-page document is not exhaustive of Houdini’s holdings but shows his deep engagement with them through his personal annotations, including his frustration at some volumes. For an 1881 edition of Thomas Frost’s The Lives of the Conjurers, for instance, he remarked: “This book is a pack of mistakes and wilful errors from the start to the finish.”

Russell, Morgan and Co (active 1867-present), poster featuring Harry Houdini in his milk can escape, 1908 Harry Houdini Papers, osf 9. Gift of the Hoblitzelle Foundation, Harry Ransom Center, The University of Texas at Austin

It was his disappointment with that book in particular that propelled Houdini’s collecting with the aim of bringing together enough primary sources to write a better record of magical history. The desire for magic to be recognised as a serious academic area of study mirrored his advocacy for the professionalisation of magic, such as serving as an early president of the Society of American Magicians.

Houdini had little formal education. Born Ehrich Weiss in 1874 in Budapest, his family immigrated to the US in 1878. They settled in Appleton, Wisconsin, where there was no public library. Yet he had formative memories of the theological books kept by his father, a rabbi.

Houdini's edition of the sermons of Bernard de Clairvaux (Strasburg: Johann Prüss, 1497) Harry Houdini Library, Incun 1497 B457. Harry Ransom Center, The University of Texas at Austin

“One of the things his father instilled in him was that having a library was a gentlemanly thing to do. It was a way of demonstrating your knowledge and that you had access to it,” Colleary says. “But you also had to be able to use it.”

Always an autodidact—revealed by his shaky spelling, like “I bot…” written inside numerous covers—books were how he first learned about magic. Reading the memoirs of the French magician Jean-Eugène Robert-Houdin inspired his adopted name. As the “Handcuff King” would later quip in an interview: “When I have come to a town, the police have tried to show me that their shackles could hold me, and have failed; the booksellers have tried to sell me many books, and have succeeded.”

Installation view of Houdini's Library at the Harry Ransom Center Photo: Trent Lesikar

On view at the Ransom Center are examples of his obsessive collecting from every angle related to magic and the stage, from Reginald Scot’s 1584 Discovery of Witchcraft—an exposé of the occult that also includes some of the first published information on sleight of hand—to broadsides advertising appearances of Henry “Box” Brown, whose great feat of illusion was escaping slavery by mailing himself in a wooden crate.

“Houdini felt very strongly that all of human knowledge was in books, and we just needed to be curious enough to go and look for it,” Colleary says. “Now with the internet, you’re so targeted and focused, you don’t get to stumble upon something you didn’t expect, and that was at the core of what Houdini loved about his collection: that ability to encounter the unexpected.”

Installation view of Houdini's Library at the Harry Ransom Center Photo: Trent Lesikar
