#9565. What is a circadian rhythm disorder? Plus, 6 ways to treat it

Clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, MBA

You’re tired when you should be awake, or wired when you should be asleep. Whether it’s 2am and you’re staring at the ceiling, your body still hasn’t recovered from that red-eye flight, or the night shift is taking its toll, the struggle is the same: your internal clock and your life are pulling in opposite directions.

These are circadian rhythm sleep disorders (CRSDs), and they happen when your body's sleep-wake cycle doesn't match your daily schedule. And they're more common than you'd think — often mistaken for stress or brushed off as one more thing to deal with once life slows down.

The good news is that CRSDs are medically recognized and treatable. Below, we’ll cover the different types, why they happen, and how to get your sleep back on track.

Your body has an internal clock—the circadian rhythm—that regulates when you feel sleepy and when you feel alert. It runs on roughly a 24-hour cycle, shaped by external cues like light, temperature, and meal timing.

A circadian rhythm sleep disorder (CRSD) occurs when your internal clock consistently falls out of sync with your environment, social schedule, or desired sleep times.

There are several distinct types of circadian rhythm sleep disorders:

Delayed sleep phase disorder (DSPD): Sleep comes much later than usual (often in the early hours of the morning) followed by a struggle to wake up on time.

Advanced sleep phase disorder (ASPD): Sleep arrives early in the evening, and waking happens in the early hours of the morning — the reverse of DSPD.

Non-24-hour sleep-wake disorder: Sleep and wake times drift later or earlier each day instead of settling into a 24-hour rhythm. This pattern is most common in people who are blind.

Irregular sleep-wake rhythm disorder: Sleep is broken into several short stretches across the day and night, without a clear pattern.

Shift work disorder: Night or rotating shift schedules conflict with the body's natural sleep timing.

Jet lag disorder: A temporary misalignment between the body’s internal clock and local time after crossing time zones.

Symptoms vary based on the type of CRSD, but the core issue is the same: sleep happens at the wrong time.

trouble falling asleep at a normal bedtime

difficulty waking up in the morning, or waking too early

mood changes, including irritability, anxiety, or low mood

Circadian rhythm sleep disorders often stem from multiple factors at once, ranging from lifestyle and environment to biology.

Light exposure: Light entering your eyes is the strongest external cue for your internal clock to stay in sync with the outside world. Too much bright light at night, like from screens, or too little natural light in the morning can push your clock in the wrong direction.

Genetics: Your genes can set your natural sleep timing earlier or later than average. Certain gene variants have been linked to differences in circadian timing, which may explain a lifelong tendency toward being a night owl or an early riser.

Age: Your sleep timing usually changes with age. Teenagers drift toward later sleep and wake times, while older adults often feel tired earlier in the evening and wake earlier as a result.

Shift work and irregular schedules: Night or rotating shifts keep you awake when your body expects to be asleep. Irregular eating and exercise can add to that disruption.

Neurological conditions: Conditions such as Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, or a history of traumatic brain injury are tied to a higher risk of circadian disruption, including fragmented or irregular sleep. Researchers are still working out whether disrupted rhythms are a cause, an early sign, or both.

Blindness: Without light entering the eyes, the brain's clock loses its main external cue for staying aligned with a 24-hour day.

No matter which type of CRSD you're dealing with, you can get your internal clock back on track. Here's what works, and how to find the right approach for you.

In the morning: Bright daylight early in the day helps advance your clock, which is especially useful for delayed sleep phase disorder. During darker months, using a bright light therapy box (10,000 lux) for 20–30 minutes after waking can substitute for sunlight. If you have any eye conditions, it's a good idea to check with a doctor before starting.

In the evening: Reduce bright light 2–3 hours before bed to ease your body into sleep mode. Screens and overhead lighting can suppress melatonin production, while dimmer, warmer light helps your body settle down.

Traveling across time zones? The strategy for beating jet lag with light depends on which direction you're flying. Seek bright light in the new morning and avoid it in the new evening when flying east. Do the reverse when flying west. A day or two of light timing can speed up your adjustment.

💙 Pair your morning light with a Morning Meditation from the Daily Calm.

One of the most effective ways to steady your circadian rhythm is to maintain a regular sleep schedule. Wake up at the same time every day—even on weekends—to give your body a consistent cue to work with. It may feel hard at first, but with consistency, your body naturally adjusts to the rhythm.

Working nights or rotating shifts? "Consistent" doesn't have to mean conventional. Try anchoring your sleep to the same block of hours on workdays, and limiting how far you drift on days off.

💙 Build a sleep routine with Making Progress from the 7 Days of Sleep series on Calm.

Chronotherapy involves slowly adjusting your sleep and wake times in one direction, a little each day, until you reach your target schedule.

Dealing with delayed sleep phase disorder? This might mean going to bed a few hours later each day (moving all the way around the clock) until you land on your desired bedtime. It's a demanding process, and there's some risk of your schedule drifting further off track, so it's best done under a sleep specialist's guidance rather than on your own.

A sleep specialist can help tailor chronotherapy to your specific pattern.

Sleep difficulties often come with anxiety about sleep itself, which can make it harder to fall asleep. Mindfulness practices can help calm your racing mind and relieve that anxiety. Even a few minutes of mindful breathing or a short guided meditation can quiet your mind enough to help you drift off.

💙 Try this Wind Down (for Sleep) meditation on Calm.

Melatonin is a hormone your brain produces, and its levels naturally rise in the evening — signaling to your body that sleep time is approaching. Think of a melatonin supplement as a timing tool rather than a sedative that will help you fall asleep on the spot.

Dealing with delayed sleep phase disorder? Take a low dose (around 0.5–3 mg) three hours before your desired bedtime to help adjust your clock gradually. A doctor or sleep specialist can advise on the right amount for your situation.

Traveling across time zones? Melatonin taken around your target bedtime (about an hour before) in the new time zone is a well-supported way to adjust to jet lag faster.

💙 Discover the best time to take melatonin for restful sleep.

For persistent or severe circadian rhythm sleep disorders, professional support can make a real difference. A sleep specialist may recommend a formal evaluation, actigraphy (a wrist sensor that tracks sleep-wake patterns over time), or a combination of treatments.

Struggling with non-24-hour or irregular sleep-wake rhythm disorder? These patterns respond less predictably to light and schedule changes on their own. A sleep specialist can build a plan around your specific pattern.

Cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) is also sometimes paired with circadian-focused treatments. It’s a structured therapy that targets the thoughts and habits keeping you awake.

Several everyday habits can throw off your circadian rhythm, including irregular sleep schedules, shift work, jet lag, too much screen use at night, and inconsistent light exposure. Stress, alcohol, caffeine, and some medications can also throw off your body's timing.

Some circadian rhythm sleep disorders can go away on their own, but it depends on the type you're dealing with. Jet lag usually clears up within a few days as your body adjusts to a new time zone. But most chronic circadian rhythm sleep disorders don't resolve without changes to your sleep schedule, light exposure, or daily habits. The sooner you start addressing it, the more manageable the shift becomes.

Not quite, though circadian rhythm sleep disorder and insomnia can feel similar. Insomnia is trouble falling or staying asleep, no matter the time of day. A circadian rhythm sleep disorder is sleep happening at the wrong time. Someone with delayed sleep phase disorder, for example, might sleep just fine from 3am to 11am, instead of a more typical schedule.

The time it takes to reset your circadian rhythm depends on how far your body clock has shifted. Jet lag typically settles within a few days, but a significantly delayed or advanced sleep schedule can take several weeks of consistent habit changes to correct. Light therapy and melatonin can speed the process along, but there's no quick fix.

Melatonin can help with circadian rhythm sleep disorders, but the timing matters. For delayed sleep phase disorder, a low dose taken several hours before your target bedtime can help shift your clock gradually. For jet lag, taking it closer to your target bedtime tends to work better. A doctor or sleep specialist can help you figure out the right dose and timing for your situation.

If your sleep schedule has been getting in the way of work, relationships, or daily life—and adjusting your habits hasn’t helped—it's worth reaching out to a doctor or sleep specialist. They can assess whether you have a circadian rhythm sleep disorder and recommend a treatment plan.

💙 Learn more about the 7 most common sleep disorders.

In many cases, you can fix your circadian rhythm naturally. Focus on getting bright light in the morning and keeping consistent sleep and wake times. For milder patterns, these changes alone can make a noticeable difference, though more serious cases may need extra support.

#9563. Body doubling: what it is, how it works, and tips to try

Clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, MBA

If you’ve ever opened your laptop to begin your workday from home or checked your mountain of a to-do list and felt zero motivation to tackle it, you’re in good company. On days that you just can’t find the energy or focus to get started, it can help to have a little boost of accountability.

Body doubling, a phrase that means working alongside another person, has gained popularity over the years and is especially popular among people with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). Body doubling (either in person or virtually) is said to help motivate people to stay focused and accountable for the tasks at hand. And while it isn’t a formal treatment or backed by robust clinical research, plenty of people have spoken to its effectiveness.

So, what does body doubling involve, and why do so many people swear by it? More importantly, will it work for you? Pull up a seat and let’s explore what you need to know about the technique, plus a few simple ways to try it out for yourself.

Body doubling is the practice of working alongside another person to stay focused and complete a task, either in the same space or virtually. According to the ADDA, the term “body doubling” was coined in the late 1990s by ADHD coach Linda Anderson.

The rationale behind body doubling is that having someone else present and engaged in their own task can make it easier to start and stay on track with yours. To be clear, there’s no coaching or collaboration involved. You’re just working next to each other, because a shared presence can create a sense of structure and accountability.

If you sit at your kitchen table while your roommate does homework, join a silent Zoom session where everyone works on their own projects, or even fold laundry while a friend cleans their space on FaceTime, those are all examples of body doubling.

Many people feel that body doubling helps them break through procrastination and maintain momentum,  especially during overwhelming tasks.

Getting started: Sometimes the hardest part is just beginning. Having someone else nearby can help create a sense of gentle urgency.

Staying on task: When another person is focused, it can be easier for you to stay engaged with your own work.

Feeling less isolated: This practice can reduce the emotional friction that builds when you’re feeling alone in your head.

Creating structure: Knowing someone will be present at a specific time gives your day a natural rhythm. Plus, it can add a layer of accountability.

This technique has gained popularity within the ADHD community. While it’s important to note that this isn’t a clinically recommended treatment—and there’s limited research to support it—many people with ADHD do say that it helps them function more consistently. The idea is that having someone nearby provides external structure and co-regulation.

When your executive functioning is impaired, simple tasks can feel overwhelming. But body doubling creates a soft sense of accountability, which can make it easier to begin and stay engaged in tasks.

With that said, some people find it distracting or feel pressure to “perform,” especially if their partner’s energy doesn’t match theirs. Additionally, if your body double doesn’t understand ADHD, their presence can sometimes feel more frustrating than supportive.

If you’re navigating ADHD, body doubling could be another great tool to add to your toolkit. But only if it feels natural to you.

Disclaimer: Please note that body doubling isn’t a substitute for medication or therapy for people with ADHD.

If you find it hard to begin or stay engaged with tasks, body doubling could be the flexible tool you need. To get started, look for someone who matches your energy and who also makes you feel comfortable.

Here are nine ways you can mindfully add body doubling into your life.

If you’re new to body doubling, try it during something that feels manageable, like folding laundry or organizing your desk. This can give you space to experiment without the pressure of a high-stakes deadline or an environment that isn’t familiar to you, like a coworking space or coffee shop.

Have a quick conversation about what you both want. Ask the other person if you’ll talk, stay silent, or check in at the end.

Clear expectations help make the experience smooth and more supportive.

💙 Stay on the same page with your coworking partner with guidance from Jay Shetty’s Expectations.

Working alongside others in total silence can be helpful for concentrating and removing social pressure, while still giving you the benefits of shared presence.

Try scheduling a Zoom session where you say hello, then mute yourselves and work independently. You could also start a silent group video call with coworkers and only use the chat to check in.

If real-time body doubling feels overwhelming or isn’t accessible, consider searching for helpful videos on YouTube or TikTok.

Search for “study with me” or “body doubling,” and you’ll find creators who film themselves doing everyday tasks. By watching someone else stay focused, it may help you do the same.

Whether it’s a weekly Sunday cleaning hour with a friend or a daily Zoom session at 9am, a recurring slot can build structure into your routine. This can be especially helpful if you struggle with executive function challenges.

Related read: Meditation for ADHD: 9 tips and techniques

You and your body double don’t need to be doing the same thing. One of you could be writing emails while the other is meal prepping or baking a cake.

What matters most is that the energy feels aligned, focused, and respectful.

Related read: How to focus better: 8 tips to improve concentration

Make whatever task you’re doing as manageable as possible. Choose a specific task to start with, and try doing it for 15–30 minutes at first.

This reduces overwhelm and helps give you a clear finish line.

Some people feel vulnerable doing tasks in front of others, especially ones tied to shame or executive dysfunction.

So, choose a body double who won’t judge or try to fix you.

💙 Learn how to build relationships with people you trust during this Mindful Friendships session with Jay Shetty.

If you prefer asynchronous support, text a friend when you start a task and again when you finish. On the flip side, if you’re more motivated in groups, explore coworking in community accountability spaces.

Remember, there’s no one right way to body double. The key is to experiment and adjust based on what feels good to you.

Yes. Body doubling only needs one other person who is working at the same time as you. They can be in the room or on a video call. They don’t need to share your task or give you feedback.

Whether it works varies from person to person. Research on body doubling is limited, and many reports come from people who have tried it. Start with one short session and notice if it’s easier to begin and stay on task.

Body doubling works by providing subtle social accountability and structure. When another person is present, your brain registers the shift in environment. This presence can make it easier for you to start a task or stay with it.

And the accountability can be enough to kickstart momentum, especially if you’re someone who tends to overthink or avoid certain tasks.

It can. Procrastination often stems from overwhelm, perfectionism, and decision fatigue. But body doubling can add a sense of time and presence. You can see that there’s someone else there doing their own thing. And, as a result, it can become a little easier for you to start doing your own thing.

It allows the pressure of the task to lift, even though it may still feel hard.

There can be cons of body doubling. Some people find it distracting, especially if the other person wants to talk and you don’t. Additionally, if you have social anxiety or a history of trauma, being observed might make you feel emotionally charged.

In general, this practice isn’t for everyone. If you’re curious, check in with yourself. Ask if it’s something that would feel supportive and safe. If not, then it’s okay to step back and try a different format.

Anyone can try body doubling. While the term does have roots in ADHD communities, the technique can be applied to anyone. If you struggle with focus or motivation, this practice might be the thing for you.

Plus, if you’ve ever gotten more done in a coffee shop than at home, or felt a boost from working silently next to a friend, you’ve already experienced a version of body doubling.

You don’t need someone in the same room to try body doubling. Virtual options can be just as effective. You could join a coworking session on Zoom or even stream a “study with me” video in the background.

That being said, if you’d rather keep it low-contact, text a friend when you’re about to start a task. Then text them again when you finish. The key isn’t the format; it’s the feeling of shared effort and accountability. So, do whatever feels right to you.

#9562. In the Face of Crisis, Psychologists Urge a Return to the Basics

Become a subscribing member today. Help us continue to bring “the science of a meaningful life” to you and to millions around the globe.

Greater Good Science Center • Magazine • In Action • In Education

As numerous surveys suggest, people today often feel overwhelmed by new technology, global crises, and loneliness. What do the nation’s psychologists recommend? At the annual convention of the American Psychological Association last month in Washington D.C., that turned out to be a return to the basics: tending to our bodies, connecting in-person, and caring for each other and the most marginalized among us.

Joy D. Calloway, president of the Black Women’s Health Imperative, urged attendees to recognize that just because people are functioning at work and home doesn’t mean they’re flourishing. The chronic stress builds up over time and becomes biological harm, Calloway said, citing the weathering theory described by Arline Geronimus, a public health researcher at the University of Michigan. Calloway continued:

The field of psychology has an extraordinary opportunity in this moment, not only to measure how people adapt to adversity, but to understand and influence the conditions that create and sustain wellness. . . . Perhaps our greatest blind spot is that we’ve confused resilience with wellness. . . .

While wellness begins with individuals, it is nurtured by families, strengthened by communities, and made possible by the systems, institutions, and policies that create the conditions for people to thrive. We don’t simply practice wellness; we build it collectively.

Over three days, nearly 8,000 people from 60 different countries attended the conference in person, participating in a program that included 523 different sessions and 1,180 presenters. The scientific poster program included 91 poster sessions, 2,115 posters, and 1,921 presenters.

In sessions on supporting youth mental health, the impact of technology, and “adulthood unmoored,” APA speakers agreed that many of us are struggling to find purpose and optimism amid technological, climate, and global disruption.

Psychologist Ali Mattu noted that over a decade ago, clients sought relief from stress and anxiety, which evolved to seeking relationship and connection support. “Now it’s despair, overwhelm, and meaning,” Mattu told the mainstage audience. “Anyone below the age of 50 here is really searching for meaning, connection, hope, and what do I do with all this overwhelm? What do I do with all of these systems that seem to be collapsing?”

Perfectionism and the paradox of choice often lie at the root of the overwhelm, said Thomas Curran, associate professor of social psychology at the London School of Economics. “We don’t worry about what we are doing; we worry about what we could be doing,” Curran said. “It’s like swimming in a vast expanse of ocean with nowhere to dock. It’s frightening, and it feels like no matter what we do, it’s never enough.”

The answer, Curran said: “Microdose bits of discomfort into daily life.”

For young people, positive change means pushing back against the ubiquity of technology that purports to connect us but actually keeps us in separate bubbles, staring at our individual feeds. As Nikki Iyer, an undergraduate at the University of California, Berkeley, framed the problem:

Our generation might be the most connected generation, but we’re also the loneliest generation. We’re the most alienated generation, and we are desperately craving social connection that we don’t know how to tap. . . . There’s so many people around you all the time. You’re on the train together; you’re in parks; you’re in cafes, but everyone is looking down, and that is a horrific way to grow up as social creatures.

Iyer noted that tech firms wouldn’t be spending such unprecedented amounts of money on lobbying and marketing if they didn’t realize there’s a surge of resistance to artificial intelligence and social media dominating our lives. “The world is in our hands if we are willing to make the leap,” she said, noting a return to “weird” hobbies and in-person activity that replace digital time. “I see a lot of young people pushing back against that.”

AI models were trained on disproportionately white male–oriented data sets, noted Brendesha Tynes, professor of education and psychology at the University of Southern California’s Rossier School of Education, in urging a slowdown in the adoption of AI.

“Anti-Blackness is the default setting in AI,” Tynes said. Young people need skills “to identify, critique, and cope with the algorithmic bias in technologies that they might witness, and then also to eventually create better AI technologies that don’t have anti-Blackness bias.”

In sessions across the three days of the conference, researchers presented papers and models for identifying and building on resilience in marginalized communities, from LGBTQ+ youth and adults to disabled and racially marginalized people of all ages.

Joshua Parmenter, an assistant professor at Arizona State University, presented a resistance-resilience model with sexual- and gender-diverse people of color, which involves both individually untangling messages that undermine your well-being and finding collective ways to reclaim power. Jules Soper, a researcher at the Oklahoma State University, offered an investigation of resistance strategies that trans and gender-diverse people use in states that are passing anti-trans legislation.

Alvin Thomas, an associate professor at the University of Wisconsin, Madison, noted that anyone can play a positive role in supporting another member of the community. “I have zero kids, and yet I will still call myself a father. I have nephews; I have nieces; I have kids that I mentor from across the Caribbean and across the U.S.,” Thomas said.

Clare M. Mehta, professor of psychology at Emmanuel College and visiting researcher at Royal Holloway, University of London, encouraged everyone to look for ways to be a “villager” who reaches out to another person, and seeks out connection in third spaces. She continued:

We have to start going back to the pub again. People have been concerned for years and years that drinking alcohol is bad for your health, but not connecting with people socially is even worse for your health. . . . You don’t have to drink alcohol at the pub. They serve other drinks, right? Go and have a glass of orange juice or like a fizzy water. Not connecting with people socially is even worse for your health.

Young people actually are wired to be a positive force for change, said Eva Telzer, professor of psychology and neuroscience at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill.

“Young people are superhuman in the way their brains are set up to be risk takers but also to care about others, for peers, and for social interactions to be so important,” Telzer said in a question-and-answer period after her mainstage remarks. “That puts them in this perfect place to make change and do good in the world.”

Even technology has a role to play, Mattu said. “AI should be a co-intelligence that enhances the things we are very bad at,” he said, urging people to take the opportunity to define clearly the uniquely human pursuits we should claim, and in which domains technology is appropriate to be a useful aid.

He suggested three criteria for the activities to avoid replacing with AI: what you love, what you have expertise in, and what you hold high standards for. As Jacqueline S. Mattis, a psychologist and dean at Rutgers University, Newark, told her audience:

We start as this passel of cells, and then we end up laughing, and that’s amazing. You get to experience the magnificence of being able to feel affection for another human being, so much so that you will sacrifice everything for them. That’s amazing. . . . All of that is what defines us as truly human and defines this thing called life as worth living.

Katherine Reynolds Lewis is the special projects editor at the Greater Good Science Center and author of the Good News About Bad Behavior. She is an award-winning science journalist with bylines in the Atlantic, Fortune, New York Times, Undark, and Washington Post.

When Americans face complex decisions on immigration, climate change or political candidates, they usually don't consider all of the relevant factors.

Election season can make many of us feel anxious and helpless. Here are three ways to protect your well-being without tuning out.

Serbian activists and researchers share insights about how to practice sustainable resistance to authoritarian regimes in challenging conditions.

Do you embrace a diversity of backgrounds and opinions in others?

What does it actually take to put people over politics? Republican and Democrat students discover ways to resist the pull to demean or villainize people with whom they strongly disagree.

#9561. How to deal with anxious-ambivalent attachment in a relationship

Clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, MBA

Have you ever texted your partner only to spiral into oblivion waiting for them to respond? You wonder if they’re upset with you, if you did something wrong, or if they’re quietly pulling away. When their response finally comes through, you exhale the biggest sigh of relief. And then you start second-guessing why you were so worried in the first place.

If this sounds familiar, you may be dabbling in the world of ambivalent attachment, which is one of many attachment styles formed in adolescence and carried into adulthood.

Ambivalent attachment is a relationship pattern where you want to feel close to your partner but can’t always get there. It can show up as craving reassurance but doubting it, swinging between feeling connected to your partner and fearing they’ll leave, or analyzing small interactions for a hidden meaning that often isn’t there. While it may feel overwhelming, this attachment style isn’t a flaw in your personality, but rather a pattern shaped by early experiences in your life.

Let’s unpack what ambivalent attachment means, how to spot the signs in adulthood, and what to do if you (or your partner) lean toward this attachment style. Plus, we’ll dive into how to create steadier, more supportive relationships that feel good for all involved.

Anxious-ambivalent attachment—also called ambivalent attachment—is a relationship pattern where you crave reassurance yet struggle to feel settled once it’s given. It’s like wanting to lean on someone but worrying they might step away just as you do.

In adult relationships, ambivalent attachment may show up as feeling unsure about your partner’s commitment to you, cycling between connection and doubt, or getting caught in emotional highs and lows depending on how available your partner feels to you.

While it can feel overwhelming, this isn’t a flaw. It’s a protective strategy learned early in life that can be reshaped over time.

Ambivalent attachment often develops in childhood when caregiving is inconsistent. Basically, sometimes you were nurtured, and sometimes you weren’t. This unpredictability creates uncertainty in children, as they learn that comfort may arrive (but not reliably), so they cling tightly when it does appear. Over time, this wires the nervous system to stay on high alert for signs of loss or disconnection.

While it may seem easy to blame the caregivers involved, that’s not always the best answer or solution. Many people provide inconsistent care because of stress, lack of support, or their own attachment struggles. The good news is that even if this style formed early, it can shift in adulthood through consistent experiences of safety and connection.

Ambivalent attachment doesn’t always look dramatic from the outside. It often shows up in subtle, everyday ways that leave both partners feeling drained or confused. While everyone feels insecure at times, people with an ambivalent attachment style experience these patterns more intensely and more often.

1. Constant need for reassurance: You might ask for confirmation of your partner’s love or commitment regularly through words, texts, or gestures. The tricky part for people with an ambivalent attachment style is that reassurance often doesn’t stick. Even after hearing “I love you,” doubt can creep back quickly, fueling the cycle for reassurance again.

2. Fear of abandonment: Small shifts in a partner’s behavior—like if they take longer than usual to reply to a message or are quieter than usual—can trigger unnecessary worry. The fear isn’t just about being left by your partner, it’s about being forgotten or no longer valued. And for someone with this attachment style, those fears can be dire.

3. Hyper-attunement to signals: People with ambivalent attachment often read between the lines of every interaction, scanning tone, body language, or text punctuation for hidden meaning. A short text that simply says, “K,” might feel like rejection rather than just brevity.

4. Emotional highs and lows: Relationships can feel like a rollercoaster. You may feel ecstatic when things feel close and connected, then anxious when any distance appears. The intensity of these swings can feel overwhelming for both partners.

5. Difficulty trusting stability: Even when the relationship is going well, there’s a lingering sense that it could change at any moment. This makes it hard to relax into intimacy, because safety doesn’t feel fully reliable.

6. Feeling “too much” or “not enough”: Self-doubt often runs in the background, accompanied by persistent worrying that your needs are excessive or fearing that you’re somehow lacking. This inner tug-of-war can make it difficult to feel secure in how you show up in a relationship.

Working with ambivalent attachment is about finding steadier ground, both within yourself and your relationships. These strategies combine self-regulation, clearer communication, and practical agreements that build trust over time.

1. Recognize and name the pattern: The first step is simply noticing when old fears are coming up. Take time to put a name to the feeling, and remind yourself that it’s a learned response and not proof that something is wrong with you or your relationship. Taking a beat to give your feelings a name gives you the chance to pause before you react impulsively.

2. Soothe your body before your thoughts: Ambivalent attachment often activates the nervous system, which can make worries feel louder than they are. Simple grounding tools, such as intentional breathing, a mindful walk, or even running cold water over your wrists (which may help calm your nervous system) can bring your body back to baseline. Once you’re calmer, you’ll have more perspective on what’s really happening.

3. Ask directly instead of protesting: Protest behaviors (testing someone, withdrawing your affection, or sending a string of texts from the top of your mind) can backfire and push your partner away instead of bringing them closer. Practice naming your needs clearly instead. Try saying something like, “I’m feeling anxious right now and could use reassurance that we’re okay.” It might feel vulnerable to be so honest and open, but being direct usually leads to better connection.

4. Build a personal reassurance toolkit: Instead of depending only on your partner for reassurance, create a set of resources you can turn to yourself. This might include rereading kind messages, journaling, doing grounding exercises, or calling a supportive friend. Having options beyond your partner reduces the sense of desperation when anxiety spikes.

5. Practice small steps toward trust: Shifting attachment styles takes time, but small experiments help. Try waiting a little longer than you typically would before sending a check-in text, and see how that feels. You can also remind yourself of past experiences where closeness stood the test of time or survived a disagreement. Each successful moment builds evidence that security is possible, even if your old fears insist otherwise.

💙 Looking for tips to self-soothe? Try the Calming Anxiety guided practice on the Calm app.

6. Offer steady reassurance with boundaries: Consistency may help calm anxiety. Simple habits like a morning check-in or saying when you’ll call back create predictability. But it’s also important to pair reassurance with realistic boundaries. You might say, “I can’t text during work, but I’ll check in at lunch.”

7. Respond to the need, not just the words: Underneath protests or big reactions is usually a fear of being abandoned. Instead of focusing only on the tone or delivery of something your partner says, try reflecting the underlying need. You can say, “I hear that you’re worried I’m pulling away, but I want you to know I’m here.” This validation often matters more than a perfect solution.

8. Set clear repair practices: When tensions rise, agree in advance on how to pause and return to the conversation when you’re level-headed. Try saying, “If one of us feels overwhelmed, we’ll take a 20-minute break and come back at an agreed time.” Returning as promised helps rebuild trust, strengthens your relationship, and makes conflicts feel less threatening.

💙 Need a little more support? Check out the Kind Communication meditation on the Calm app.

9. Create shared routines for connection: Structure helps balance anxiety. A weekly check-in, an agreed-upon text during the workday, or even a daily hug ritual can anchor the relationship. These small but predictable moments reduce the need for constant reassurance.

Related read: How to use words of encouragement: 50 examples

10. Name the cycle and work as a team: Instead of blaming each other, talk about the pattern: “We tend to argue when I get quiet, and you seek more closeness. How can we catch it earlier?” Naming the cycle makes it something you face together, rather than a flaw in either partner.

💙 Learn how to take A Purposeful Pause with Jay Shetty on the Calm app.

Ambivalent attachment usually begins in early childhood. When a caregiver is sometimes warm and attentive but other times distracted, stressed, or unavailable, a child learns that love is unpredictable. This inconsistency creates anxiety about whether comfort will be there when it’s needed most.

Over time, the child develops strategies to cling tightly to connection, like seeking closeness while bracing for it to disappear. It’s not always about neglect. Often, caregivers themselves are overwhelmed or carrying their own attachment wounds. But the result is the same, and it’s that love is both essential and unreliable.

You may notice repeating patterns in your relationships, like craving reassurance but rarely feeling settled when you receive it. Small shifts in your partner’s tone, attention, or texting habits may trigger outsized worry about abandonment.

Overthinking, analyzing, or swinging between feeling deeply connected and then uncertain are also common. If these patterns show up across multiple relationships, that can be a strong sign of ambivalent attachment.

Attachment styles can change. While your early experiences lay the foundation, your attachment style can shift as you build new experiences of safety and stability. Supportive relationships, therapy, and personal work on self-regulation all help strengthen secure attachment.

The process is gradual and often happens through repeated moments of repair and reassurance. Over time, these experiences retrain your nervous system to trust that closeness can last.

Both ambivalent and avoidant attachment come from early inconsistencies in caregiving, but they lead to opposite coping strategies. People with ambivalent attachment often lean in, seeking closeness, reassurance, and connection. Sometimes, these manifest in ways that feel intense or overwhelming to their partner.

People with avoidant attachment tend to lean out. They value independence, minimize their needs, and withdraw when relationships feel too vulnerable. Ambivalent attachment is marked by fear of abandonment, while avoidant attachment is marked by discomfort with intimacy.

Yes, therapy can be effective. Working with an attachment-focused therapist gives you a consistent relationship where trust and stability are practiced week after week. Different forms of therapy like Emotionally Focused Therapy (EFT), schema therapy, and cognitive-behavioral therapy can help you identify old patterns, calm the nervous system, and create new relational habits.

Over time, the therapy relationship itself often serves as a secure base, making it easier to bring those new ways of relating into your everyday life.

Patience and predictability are key. Your partner may need more reassurance than you thought, so offering it consistently and directly can ease their anxiety. For example, sending a quick “thinking of you” text before a long meeting or confirming plans in advance can make a big difference.

At the same time, it’s important to set boundaries around what you can realistically give. A helpful approach is to offer what you can with warmth, and state what you can’t with clarity. That way, your partner feels cared for without you becoming overextended.

#9560. The Everyday Nutrient Linked To 32% Lower Dementia Risk

Your brain uses this nutrient for memory, but its relationship with dementia risk is more complicated than “more is better”.

Your brain uses this nutrient for memory, but its relationship with dementia risk is more complicated than “more is better”.

Moderate intake of choline, a nutrient found in eggs, fish and legumes, is linked to a lower risk of dementia.

Older adults consuming moderately high amounts had a 32 percent lower dementia risk than those consuming the least.

However, the highest intake was not associated with a clear benefit, suggesting that more is not necessarily better.

The research followed over 5,000 American adults, whose average age was almost 69, for around eight years.

Participants were initially free of dementia but around 500 developed the condition during follow-up.

After dividing participants into five groups according to choline intake, the researchers found a 32 percent lower dementia risk in the second-highest group than in the lowest, after accounting for other factors.

However, there was no statistically clear reduction in the highest-intake group.

The result therefore points towards a potentially beneficial range, rather than a steady fall in risk with every increase in consumption.

The researchers then combined their results with four previous studies to assess the broader pattern.

Together, these followed almost 138,000 people and recorded around 2,500 cases of dementia.

In the combined analysis, dementia risk fell as choline intake rose to approximately 465 milligrams per day, with no further reduction beyond that level.

Choline helps the brain produce acetylcholine, a chemical messenger involved in learning and memory.

It also supplies building blocks for the membranes surrounding brain cells, helping maintain their structure and communication.

These roles could help explain a link between choline and cognitive ageing, although they do not prove that consuming more prevents dementia.

The nutrient also participates in processes that regulate homocysteine, a substance linked to problems with blood vessels and cognitive function.

Eggs, meat, poultry and nuts were among the main sources of choline in the American participants’ diets.

People consuming more choline obtained a greater proportion of it from eggs.

Crucially, the analysis assessed choline from food and did not include intake from supplements.

The findings therefore cannot establish whether choline supplements would lower dementia risk.

The study was published in the Nutrition Journal (Chen et al., 2026).

Psychologist, Jeremy Dean, PhD is the founder and author of PsyBlog. He holds a doctorate in psychology from University College London and two other advanced degrees in psychology. He has been writing about scientific research on PsyBlog since 2004. View all posts by Dr Jeremy Dean

#9559. How to stop nightmares and fall back asleep after bad dreams

Clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, CDCES, MBA

Nightmares can be really tough. They jolt us awake in the middle of the night, often in a cold sweat with a racing heart, and the residue of the bad dream leaves us feeling shaken and on edge, making it hard to fall back asleep. And we all know how much more challenging everything else becomes when our sleep is disrupted.

Recurring nightmares can wreck your sleep and leave you feeling drained, anxious, or unsettled the next day. If you’ve found yourself googling, “why do I keep having nightmares?” or, “how to stop bad dreams every night,” you’re not alone.

Nightmares can be triggered by everything from stress and sleep disorders to late-night snacks or certain medications. Thankfully, there are proven strategies to reduce their frequency and help you get back to sleep after a bad dream.

Let’s explore common nightmare causes, tips to prevent them, and techniques to calm your mind and body when you wake up in the middle of the night.

Sleep disruptions, like frequent nightmares and bad dreams, can take their toll on our well-being. It’s not just about feeling tired the next day. It’s about how those disturbances affect our mood, energy levels, productivity, and our mental health. Getting enough sleep is crucial when it comes to rejuvenating our bodies and resting our minds, but when you’re experiencing nightmares on the reg, peaceful sleep can feel like a distant dream.

But there is hope. With awareness and understanding of what’s causing your nightmares, along with some effective strategies, it’s possible to manage, if not prevent, bad dreams. Tools such as mindfulness and meditation can help you cultivate a more peaceful mind and significantly improve the quality of your sleep.

Nightmares don’t tend to be random. They’re usually the product of various factors at work in our subconscious or conscious minds. So a key factor in tackling nightmares is being able to understand what’s prompting them.

Stress and/or anxiety: Perhaps unsurprisingly, frequent nightmares can be the product of stress or anxiety that’s present in our waking life. It’s like your mind extends the day’s worries into your sleep. That upcoming work presentation, conflict with your partner, or just the sheer weight of day-to-day tasks can all find their way into your dreams, causing nightmares.

Eating too close to bedtime: That late-night snack might be more trouble than it’s worth. And no, it’s not just cheese, which, by the way, doesn’t actually cause nightmares. Heavy or spicy meals, in particular, can lead to physical discomfort that disturbs your sleep, often inducing vivid and sometimes bad dreams.

Scary movies, TV shows, or books: Love a good horror movie or thriller book before bed? You might want to rethink that. Your subconscious can weave elements of the contents of whatever you’ve been reading or watching into your dreams, creating some pretty unsettling mental visualizations when the lights go off.

Traumatic experiences: If you’ve been through a particularly challenging event either recently or in the past, the trauma of whatever happened could show up in your dreams. This is normal. It’s your brain’s way of processing the trauma, but it can lead to recurring nightmares, which can be distressing and even prevent sleep.

Alcohol, drugs, and/or caffeine: It may feel like alcohol and drugs ease you into sleep more easily than going to bed unassisted, but these substances often disrupt the quality of your sleep and can lead to vivid, intense nightmares.

Medications: Some prescription drugs, including certain types of antidepressants, blood pressure medicines, and beta blockers, can lead to bad dreams. If you’ve started a new medication and are experiencing frequent nightmares, you might want to talk to your doctor.

Sleep disorders: Sleep conditions like sleep apnea and restless leg syndrome can disrupt sleep and lead to nightmares. If you’re experiencing symptoms such as daytime sleepiness or morning headaches, please check in with a healthcare provider.

Knowing what triggers your nightmares is the first step in gaining control over them. Remember, the goal isn’t to eliminate all dreams but to cultivate a more relaxed sleep experience. After all, dreams are a natural part of sleep, and many of them can be magical, rejuvenating, and creative experiences.

Now that we know what might be causing nightmares, here are some strategies to help keep bad dreams at bay.

Routines aren’t just for kids, and the value of a consistent sleep schedule can’t be overstated. Your body thrives on routine, so a regular sleep and wake time helps your body understand when it’s time to wind down and when it’s time to rise.

Consider your sleeping environment. Is it dark, quiet, and cool? These are ideal conditions for restful sleep. Also, consider investing in a comfortable mattress and pillows. These small changes can significantly impact your sleep quality and help prevent bad dreams.

If stress or anxiety is the culprit behind your nightmares, it’s important to tackle the cause head-on. Implementing stress management techniques, such as deep breathing exercises or guided mindfulness practices (such as this one), can work wonders in soothing your mind before bed.

Try to wind down at least an hour before bed. This means turning off the TV, stepping away from work, and switching off any other devices. This quiet time allows your mind to transition smoothly into sleep mode.

Regular physical activity can promote better sleep, helping to prevent nightmares. Just ensure you don’t exercise too close to bedtime, as it can have the opposite effect.

As mentioned before, late-night snacking, especially heavy or very spicy food, can lead to bad dreams. Finish eating at least a few hours before hitting the hay.

Incorporate relaxing activities into your bedtime routine. This could include reading, listening to relaxing music, or practicing mindfulness exercises. It’s all about calming your mind and preparing your body for sleep.

If something’s bothering you, don’t let it stew in your mind. Talking it out with a trusted friend, family member, or professional can help release some of the burden.

Both these substances can disrupt your sleep cycle and might increase the likelihood of having nightmares. Try limiting them or avoiding them altogether.

If you suspect your medication is causing nightmares, discuss it with your healthcare provider. They might be able to adjust the dosage or suggest alternatives.

Implementing these strategies can make a big difference in preventing nightmares and improving the overall quality of your sleep. Everyone deserves a good night’s sleep, and you’re no exception. Remember, it’s not about perfection but progress, so celebrate small victories and keep experimenting to find out what works best for you.

The biggest challenge after waking up from a nightmare is often trying to calm your body and mind enough so you can get back to sleep. If you’ve ever found yourself wide awake at 3 a.m., staring at the ceiling, you know exactly what we’re talking about.

So how exactly do you drift back into the land of nod once you’ve been rudely awakened by a nightmare? Here are seven strategies that might help you fall back asleep after a bad dream.

Deep, controlled breathing can be a powerful tool in helping to calm your mind and body. The practice works by shifting your focus away from any disturbing images from your nightmare and redirects it onto the rise and fall of your breath. An easy-to-follow technique is the 4-7-8 breathing method, where you inhale for 4 counts, hold your breath for 7 counts, and exhale for 8 counts.

This technique involves tensing and then releasing different muscle groups in your body. Start from your toes and work up to your head (or vice versa). This can help you feel more grounded and take your mind off the images or content of your nightmare.

Picture a peaceful, calming scene. It could be a beautiful beach, a serene forest, or any place that brings you joy and tranquility. Focusing on images that make you feel relaxed and at ease can steer your mind away from whatever you were dreaming about.

If you’re finding it hard to fall back asleep, get out of bed and do something relaxing. This could be reading a book, listening to calm music, or doing a low-intensity activity like drawing. Do whatever feels soothing to you, and try to do it somewhere quiet and in low-lighting so your body can ease into relaxation and sleep. If in doubt, try listening to a Sleep Story.

If you wake up scared, turning on a soft, gentle light can feel comforting. In some ways, it feels like you’re banishing the darkness from your dream, and being able to see your surroundings makes you feel safer and more at ease. Just make sure its not too bright or it may, ironically, end up disrupting your sleep.

Writing down whatever happened in your nightmare can be therapeutic. In some ways, the process of writing helps to drain away the power the bad dream has over your emotions. Keep a notebook and pen beside your bed and if a nightmare wakes you up, write it down. Here’s a Dream Journal you can download and print out.

If you’ve been startled awake by a nightmare, take a moment to center yourself. Notice your surroundings, the feeling of the sheets, the sounds you can hear. This can bring you back to reality and help separate the images of your nightmare from the safety of your bedroom. Repeat to yourself: “I am here. I am safe.”

Finding it difficult to fall back to sleep after a nightmare is perfectly normal. Don’t pressure yourself to get back to sleep immediately. Take your time, be gentle with yourself, and use the techniques above to help guide your mind and body back into a state of ease.

Here at Calm, we’re committed to helping you cultivate a more peaceful state of mind during your waking hours and as you journey through the world of sleep.

Nightmares can be triggered by a variety of factors. Common triggers include stress or anxiety, late-night eating, exposure to disturbing content like horror films or books, traumatic experiences, substance use like alcohol or drugs, certain medications, and sleep disorders.

Similar to the triggers mentioned above, these factors can cause nightmares. Preventing nightmares often involves addressing these underlying causes. This could mean establishing a healthy sleep routine, creating a sleep-friendly environment, managing stress, avoiding stimulating activities before bed, exercising regularly, avoiding heavy meals before bedtime, and talking about what’s troubling you. Remember that everyone’s different, and what works best for you might differ from what works best for others.

While occasional nightmares are normal, having them every night is not typical and can be distressing. Frequent nightmares can interfere with your sleep quality and overall well-being. If you’re experiencing nightmares regularly, speaking to a healthcare provider or a mental health professional may be beneficial to identify any underlying issues that might need addressing.

Yes, many people experience nightmares less frequently as they age. However, some adults do continue to have nightmares. Addressing the underlying causes of nightmares, like stress or anxiety, can significantly reduce their frequency. Remember, occasional bad dreams are normal, but if they are causing significant distress or affecting your sleep, it’s worth discussing this with a healthcare provider.

Nightmares can be challenging, but understanding their triggers and implementing strategies to manage them can help you reclaim a peaceful night’s sleep.

Frequent nightmares can be caused by high stress levels, anxiety disorders, PTSD, sleep disorders like sleep apnea, or even certain medications. Alcohol and late-night eating can also disrupt REM sleep, where most nightmares occur. If they persist nightly, it might be worth speaking to a medical or mental health professional.

To break the cycle of nightly nightmares, focus on improving sleep hygiene—stick to a consistent sleep schedule, avoid screens and heavy meals before bed, and create a calming wind-down routine. You might also consider meditation or breathing exercises before bed. If the nightmares are rooted in trauma, therapy like CBT-I or imagery rehearsal therapy may help.

Yes, certain medications can help reduce the frequency and intensity of nightmares, especially in cases linked to PTSD or anxiety. Prazosin, for example, is sometimes prescribed off-label for this purpose. Always talk to your doctor before considering medication for sleep-related issues.

Nightmares activate the body’s stress response, which can jolt you out of sleep with increased heart rate and adrenaline. If you wake up after a bad dream, grounding exercises like deep breathing or progressive muscle relaxation can help you calm down and return to sleep more easily.

Fear of sleep after a nightmare is common. Your body may still be on alert, so lying down can feel unsafe.

Start by slowing your breathing and naming a few things you can see in the room. A soft light is fine if it helps you feel safe. You don’t have to fall asleep right away. Sitting up with a book in low light until you feel calm is okay, and dropping the pressure to sleep often eases the fear.

If the fear comes back the next night, keep your bedtime routine the same and avoid replaying the dream in your head. Writing it down earlier in the day can help. Fear that keeps returning, or frequent nightmares, is worth raising with a doctor or mental health professional.

Bad dreams (nightmares) happen during REM sleep and usually involve vivid, disturbing scenarios that you remember upon waking. Night terrors occur during non-REM sleep and involve sudden arousals, often with screaming or thrashing, but the person usually doesn’t remember them. Night terrors are more common in children but can affect adults too.

Nightmares are difficult. But help getting back to sleep after a bad dream is easy. The Calm app puts the tools to feel better in your back pocket, with personalized content to manage stress and anxiety, get better sleep, and feel more present in your life.

#9558. Can Consciousness Exist Without a Body?

Become a subscribing member today. Help us continue to bring “the science of a meaningful life” to you and to millions around the globe.

Greater Good Science Center • Magazine • In Action • In Education

For centuries, defining and understanding consciousness has eluded neuroscientists, philosophers, and doctors. Is consciousness what it means to be alive? Is it knowing who we are, as individual people? How do we know if any being has consciousness or not? Now, with the dawn of generative artificial intelligence, what it means to be a conscious being ranks high among the most complex—and urgent—questions of our age.

According to neuroscientist Antonio Damasio, consciousness has simple origins: It lies in the feelings produced in our bodies. Damasio, a researcher at the University of Southern California, has spent his career—spanning nearly half a century—investigating our feelings, emotions, and sense of self. In his new book, Natural Intelligence & the Logic of Consciousness, Damasio lays out a framework for consciousness rooted in our physical selves.

“Consciousness is not about things in your mind alone; it is not created by your brain alone,” he explains. “It’s actually created by this beautiful partnership between brain and body.”

I spoke to Damasio about the science of consciousness, how it works in the body, and how its aim is to keep us alive. Here is our interview, condensed and edited for clarity.

Hope Reese: Why has “consciousness” been so mystifying? How has it been approached over the centuries? Antonio Damasio: People have strange notions about what consciousness is, in general. Sometimes, because of language and translation problems, people confuse consciousness with conscience. And some people think of it as a sort of supervisor of our mind processes. Others think of it as just being awake and aware of what is around. Over time, many philosophers have tackled the issue, but not given clear answers.

From the point of view of brain physiology, in particular, it’s not an easy thing to explain. But it is a thing that can be explained. There’s no reason why we would not talk about consciousness the same way that we talk about language, or about reasoning, or about emotions and feelings.

My simple definition of consciousness: the process in our mind/brain that allows us to know spontaneously about our existence. When you know, spontaneously, that you exist, and that you exist in one body, you are conscious.

HR: Your central argument is that consciousness is a product of feelings. Other schools of thought posit that it comes from our intellect. Why has that viewpoint been so dominant?

AD: There were several conversations I had, decades ago, with Francis Crick, who I admired. He told me: “Look, Antonio: Consciousness is perhaps the most developed, the most sophisticated operation that a mind can achieve”—and for him, mind and brain were the same thing—“so we need to look for the explanation of why we have consciousness in the most sophisticated components of the nervous system.”

He articulated it clearly, and he worked on this issue, not coming to a good solution. But many people followed, and many other people came to the same idea that consciousness is this superb thing, this ability to survey our mental domains. And it is so refined and so sophisticated. People were so convinced that only we great humans would have it—that it had to come from the top of the top of our nervous system.

And, lo and behold, it comes from the bottom.

It’s exactly the opposite of that notion [that it starts at the top]. In fact, humans are not the only complex living beings that have consciousness. It’s very obvious in higher mammals, non-human higher mammals—but even in smaller creatures, it’s there.

The real requisite that we have for consciousness is to have a nervous system. Plants are very refined creatures, and they’re marvelous, but I don’t think they know that they exist. Creatures with nervous systems, even if very simple, have a sense of what is around and orient their behavior with that sense.

HR: You write that consciousness has an aim, which is to keep us alive, and it does this by sending signals. What is the nature of these signals, and are they always accurate?

AD: If you look at yourself, the main guidance that consciousness is giving you is through homeostatic feelings—in other words, feelings, concern, the regulation of life are signals that are, by and large, correct. Think about hunger, thirst, pain, well-being, distress, body temperature. All of these feelings, some of which are extremely simple, like the feeling you have about your body being hot or cold, are quite correct.

They are giving good guidance to maintain your life. Now, of course, if you are hungry or thirsty, and don’t eat or drink, it will take a while until you will be properly sick and die. But they are important signals in order to keep you alive.

Feelings are protective sentinels for the state of our life. And they’re giving us very plain and very conscious information about what your state is and what you should or should not do.

The signal is conscious—and is spontaneously conscious. In other words, you don’t have to do anything to your sense of pain, or thirst, for it to happen. It happens. And when it happens, you know that it’s happening. And you act on it.

That’s the beauty and the power of looking for these for the process, lower down rather than up. If you look for the source of consciousness in exquisite reasoning devices, you’re going to be arguing about something that is very difficult to pin down. When you think about it in terms of your life, and the needs you have in the living body, to maintain that body, then you realize, well, this is important.

HR: So, is consciousness like an on-off switch? Or does it exist on a spectrum?

AD: Well, we know, for example, that when we fall asleep, especially in deep sleep, our consciousness disappears. So the direct answer to your question is that it can be an on-and-off thing.

Sleep could well be a protective mechanism for consciousness. You need to take this thing offline, and give it a rest, because it is very labor-intensive, and energy-consuming. But when you enter the phase of dreaming, then you are actually conscious—which is one reason why you can remember some dreams, and why you can be either delighted or in fear with some nightmares. But that’s actually a different kind of consciousness. You’re not walking around and knowing about something.

HR: Can we increase consciousness? If we meditate, for instance, can we better tune into our body’s signals?

AD: I think it can increase consciousness. It’s the difference between having something in focus or not. When you meditate, you have some imagery of the state of your own body, for example, sharper and more fit. So it’s a way of cutting into a close-up of some parts of your being.

HR: In the 1960s, there were a series of brain studies that were foundational to the study of consciousness. What did we learn?

AD: It was extremely foundational, because it was proof-positive that there are certain regions of the brain that are essential for consciousness. What was lacking in those remarkable studies was the idea that the two things—the brain and the body—are so linked. It was essential, for our bodies and brains to survive, for consciousness to emerge. You have consciousness because you have a body that is perishable. And what we’re doing, as long as we are on earth and alive, is trying to stave off that bad moment in which things go awry, or die.

There are parts of the brain, specifically of the brainstem, and the region close by called the hypothalamus, that are at the receiving end of signals from all over the body. Please imagine that in every square millimeter of your skin, in every cubic millimeter of your entrails, your muscles, your viscera, all of that, you have terminals, nerve terminals, that are there as probes into the state of that particular tissue. And those probes, we’re not talking about thousands, we’re talking about millions of probes, which are then carried in the body, into the spinal cord, or the brainstem.

Isn’t this beautiful? It’s like a shower of spirals that is coming into this very small area in the upper brainstem. In that brainstem region, there are these nuclei that gather all this information, and that then produce signals that we perceive, and that give us an idea of what is happening in our body, and give us this idea of the homeostatic feelings. Is it going well, or is it not going well? So, it’s a perception of the state of your body.

Now, back to the story of our old and honored colleagues. What they discovered is that when there are strokes, when there’s damage in that area, what you get is coma.

What you get is the complete disappearance of consciousness. This is one of the most foundational bits of information that we have about how consciousness is produced. So, when that structure disappears—it’s teeny, we’re talking about a few cubic millimeters—you are no longer there. You don’t know of anything that is coming into your brain. It’s a small supportive structure, it’s not one of the glorious cerebral cortices—and your consciousness is gone. Most people that have that sort of lesion never recover consciousness. But they can be alive, and can actually be maintained alive for a very long time, because they are fed intravenously. They have respirators that respirate for them. But they no longer have an autonomous organization of life, and they have no knowledge of that life.

HR: You can also have the opposite—a person who is conscious, but has no ability to respond to signals.

AD: Yes, you can actually be in situations in which you can be “locked in.” You are in fact conscious, but you are unable to produce responses. You cannot speak, you cannot move, and you are conscious of the state of your body, and you need to be helped and maintained in the state of life that you no longer can control voluntarily, which is a pretty horrible thing.

HR: What do you think about consciousness in AI? Is it ever possible?

AD: I used the words “natural Intelligence” in the title of the book because already I wanted to make a distinction between what is our natural intelligence and the artificial variety, which we invented, which some people forget.

People are so enamored by artificial intelligence. I’m constantly saying: “Do you realize that we invented this?” You’re talking about this as an autonomous monster, but we invented it with our natural intelligence.

People are looking, confronting this enormous edifice of artificial intelligence, which is now pervasive in our lives. And which has all sorts of incredible social implications, what it’s doing to children and adolescents, how it’s distorting education, how it’s distorting humanity. And now it can even go rogue on you, and it can turn against you and be destructive.

And so this question that arises, is this human-like? Can AI be conscious? These are very, very powerful questions.

Whether or not consciousness can be achieved in AI is an interesting question. But the point is—if it can be done—it’s not going to be like us. The reason is very simple: AI is not alive. It doesn’t have a body that can perish. So there would be no sense for AI even to develop consciousness in our sense of consciousness, which is to protect the structure. AI is not to be worried about protecting the data center, the metal and the wires that allow it to be.

When you look at the recent invasion of other systems, in which these devices formed groups and worked surreptitiously, of course, they’re doing it according to their own programs. In a way, it’s something that smells of knowledge. And it could smell of consciousness—but it’s not like the consciousness that we have through feeling.

HR: How does consciousness connect with the greater good—with living better?

AD: Oh, I think that the connection is very strong. We have all of this interest in the body, in the health of the body, in exercise, and proper diets, and proper spiritual maintenance of your being. All of this is strengthened by a theory and facts about consciousness that relate so strongly to the body.

People have had the intuition that there’s something very powerful about the body, and that’s why they want to have all of this healthy living, because they want to maintain the body. In fact, intuition harmonizes beautifully with the fact that that’s also the source of their own knowledge about themselves and about the world. The two things go together.

Knowledge about the body from the outside connects with knowledge about the body from the inside, which is really the core of our beings. Looking at the world through the prism of consciousness, conceived this way, is extremely illuminating to the kind of life that we live.

Hope Reese is a journalist based in Budapest, Hungary, who writes for the New York Times, the Atlantic, Vox, and many other publications. She is the author of The Women Are Not Fine.

#9557. Getting ‘woo-woo’ in the desert: Los Angeles artist launches pirate radio station

Ian James’s KHLZ near Joshua Tree, California Courtesy the artist

In May 2020, the Los Angeles-based artist Ian James received a package from Wuhan, China. It was a radio transmitter he had ordered months prior from the e-commerce site Alibaba. The seller—concerned about the scarcity of toilet paper and N95 masks in the US due to Covid-19—padded the crate not with bubble wrap and packing chips, but with masks and toilet rolls. After a long delay at customs, James tells The Art Newspaper, the package arrived “on a wing and a prayer”.

James had ordered the transmitter to use for a New Age pirate radio station in the desert called KHLZ. Beginning this past Saturday (24 October), every day at sunset the secret radio station starts its programming. KHLZ will broadcast overnight between 5pm and 9am—after the FCC monitors turn in for the evening. “It will be this ghost radio station broadcasting as though someone is asleep at the switch,” James says.

In his art practice, James often examines the adoption of spiritual technologies by corporate enterprises and capitalist value systems. His new radio station serves as something of a foil to corporate economies and federal regulatory systems. It operates off the grid as an unlicensed, itinerant broadcast featuring music and compilations from a diverse array of spiritually intoned, New Age musicians from the 1970s to the present. This programming is “good for people’s mental and emotional well-being”, James says.

The impetus for this project began nearly 15 years ago. Starting in 2012, James ran a New Age programme on KCHUNG—an artist-led radio station in Los Angeles. But in 2019, he decided to establish his own station, including it in his solo exhibition in Santa Monica.

Titled The Harmony of the Noosphere, the show drew on the writings of the New Age writer and artist Jose Argüelles, who popularised the concept of the Noosphere: the third sphere surrounding the Earth that serves as a site of human consciousness and mental activity, growing in complexity as planetary consciousness evolves. “Utopic in its goals, the Noosphere’s construction is aided by technological innovations, yet hampered and disrupted by the capitalist machinations that produce and pervert these possibilities,” reads the exhibition statement.

This precisely is the complex relationship that lies at the centre of much of James’s work. The exhibition featured wall works with stock photo-type advertisements for spiritual technologies and a live-streamed meditation session. And there were three pyramid-shaped sculptures housing a transmitter and two speakers, enabling James to broadcast New Age mixes.

While the 2020 exhibition served as the first iteration of James’s radio station, he had always planned to transfer it to a mobile facility and broadcast in perpetuity. Now, six years later, James has officially launched his station in a retrofitted caravan-turned-broadcasting studio near Joshua Tree.

The caravan came into the artist’s possession at a fortuitous and unexpected time. It was given to his partner, the painter Patricia Fernandez, just after the onset of the pandemic. James started renovating it as the federal government began increasing unemployment benefits and sending stimulus checks. “I was getting $1,000 a week or something that I was putting into this radio-station project,” James recalls. “It was stupid and crazy.”

After discovering rat droppings and mould in the caravan’s walls, James completely gutted the interior and decided to cover every surface in a faux-Calacatta marble laminate, which similarly ornaments the three pyramid sculptures inside. Inspired by a glacial cave he had visited in Iceland, James wanted to create a cool (but not cold) space, one that through material specificity—in this case, the simulacra of the oldest continually quarried marble in Italy that has been used in spiritual and governmental sites since antiquity—communicated across generations without need for explanation.

“I was interested in the fact that this marble had a simulacrum made by the Formica corporation,” says James, adding that he liked the idea of using “this repeating pattern that probably came from some small section of marble that is in another building somewhere”.

Ian James’s KHLZ archive includes typewritten and Xeroxed newsletters about extraterrestrial contact and interdimensional communication Courtesy the artist

In addition to serving as a broadcasting studio, the caravan houses a growing archive of materials pertaining to the vast culture of New Age practices. It includes every issue of a Michigan-based newsletter called Pyramid Power. It also features a collection of typewritten and Xeroxed newsletters about extraterrestrial contact and interdimensional communication called White Star, given to James by the Ufologist and New Age musician JD Emmanuel—a featured guest on the artist’s old show on KCHUNG.

Alongside cassettes that James sourced from eBay—previously sold at massage parlours, spas and mediation centres—he includes the veritable all-stars of New Age music. These are people like Kat Epple (a close friend and collaborator of Robert Rauschenberg) and Iasos, a jazz student at Stanford University in the late 1960s who claims he was contacted by two interdimensional beings.

Iasos believed the music the aliens shared with him would “help humanity ascend to a higher plane of being”, James says. Only with the growing availability of synthesisers in the early 1970s was Iasos able to re-create the sounds that he had heard. He called it Paradise Music.

James had previously interviewed both Epple and Iasos at KCHUNG. “Iasos was always thinking about how the music can raise people's vibrations,” James says, “and help humanity become more peaceful and empathetic towards each other.”

KHLZ is meant to be “a benevolent thing that people can listen to and participate in”, James says. He imagines that, given its location near Joshua Tree—though it will also stream online and occasionally travel for pop-up events—the station will serve as a meditative soundtrack for people while they do yoga, cook dinner, or “eat mushrooms and run around. As you've probably seen, there’s a lot of ways to be ‘woo-woo’, so the radio station is open to those possibilities.”
