#9556. How to be more productive: 6 tips to help you get things done

Clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, MBA

You start your day with a plan: clear your to-do list, get ahead, maybe even sign off early. Instead, your attention gets pulled in every direction. Back-to-back calls, a stream of emails, countless tabs open at once. Next thing you know, the day's almost over, your list is still full, and you're left wondering how you’re supposed to get anything done.

Busyness and productivity can look identical from the outside, but they’re not the same. You can stay busy all day tackling small, urgent-feeling tasks without ever touching the work that really counts. Being productive means doing the tasks that matter, which requires staying intentional about where your time and energy go.

So what's getting in the way of your productivity, and what can you do about it? Here’s a closer look at the everyday friction that can slow you down, plus a few shifts to help you make the most of each day.

Most productivity drains are minor, routine points of friction that are easy to miss, yet they add up fast. A few usual suspects:

Context switching: Research shows that every jump between tasks costs you the time it takes to mentally reset, even when it feels instant.

Constant interruptions: Responding to notifications and drop-in requests can feel productive, but it turns your attention to other people's priorities.

Unclear priorities: When everything feels urgent, you often default to whatever's quickest instead of what matters most.

Running on empty: Skipping breaks seems like it saves time, but it slows you down later and wears down your focus.

Procrastination: When a task feels overwhelming or unclear, it’s tempting to reach for something more manageable instead of starting the job you need to do.

Good news: you can reduce these points of friction without turning your whole day upside down. The tips below aren’t a set system, just a few ideas you can implement on your own terms. Start with one or two, and notice what feels different.

Decide what would make today count before you open your inbox. Not five things, just one that matters most. Write it down somewhere visible, then dedicate the first stretch of your day to that task before anything else pulls your focus away.

💙 Start your day mindfully with this Finding Focus practice on Calm.

Multitasking may feel efficient, but your brain can’t really do two things at once. It's switching fast between them, and each switch costs you a little focus and energy. Over a full day, those costs add up.

Try working in single-task blocks. Close the extra tabs, silence your phone, and stay with one task until it's done or you hit a natural stopping point. You'll often finish faster than if you’d juggled three tasks at once.

💙 Learn more with Jay Shetty’s Settle Down by Single-Tasking session on Calm.

The apps and platforms you use are built to stretch your attention in a dozen directions. Every ping invites you to switch tasks, and you’re driven to take the bait without thinking twice.

You don't have to go off-grid to take back control. Check your email at two or three set times instead of leaving it open. Turn off notifications you don't need, and put your phone in another room during focused work. If one site keeps tempting you, a browser blocker can hold the line.

💙 Explore Digital Distractions from the 7 Days of Focus series on Calm.

Your focus isn't a tap you can leave running. If you push too long without pausing, your attention frays, mistakes creep in, and even small tasks can start to feel hard.

Try working in stretches of about 25 minutes, then step away to stretch, breathe, or look out a window. It’s also worth protecting your downtime in the evenings and on weekends, so you're not completely drained by mid-week.

💙 Dr. Alex Pang makes the case for smarter rest in The Power of Rest, a Calm masterclass.

Your to-do list is probably a mix of very different kinds of work. A report needs deep focus. A stack of emails or calls may not need any. Some work requires creativity, while some mainly requires attention to detail. Tackling tasks in a random order means starting cold, over and over.

But if you batch similar tasks, you can move through them while you're already warmed up for that type of work. Keep your quick replies to a couple of set windows instead of scattered across the day, and stack your calls so they run one after another. Once you're in the groove of one kind of work, staying there beats starting over.

A task tends to stretch to fill whatever time you give it. Timeboxing flips that. You pick a task, decide up front how long it gets—say 30 minutes—then stop when the time runs out, whether you're finished or not. That cap keeps one email from swallowing a whole morning, and stops you from polishing something long past the point of diminishing returns.

It also takes the guesswork out of what comes next, since you've chosen in advance. Block the slot on your calendar and set a timer. When the box closes, decide consciously whether the task gets another round.

💙 If starting is the hardest part, these 9 techniques can help you stop procrastinating.

You can train yourself to be more productive by gradually incorporating new helpful habits, like choosing a top priority for the day, single-tasking, and reducing digital distractions. Start with one small change and repeat it until it feels natural. One well-known study found that a new behavior took an average of 66 days to feel automatic—ranging from 18–254 days depending on the person—so give yourself time to adjust.

Yes, people with ADHD often struggle with productivity, and it’s not about effort or willpower. ADHD involves differences in executive function, the mental skills you use to start tasks, plan, and hold attention. This is why even starting tasks you want to do can feel difficult. The strategies in this article are still useful, though you may need to adapt them to what works for your brain.

💙 If ADHD is getting in the way of your work, here’s more on why that happens and how to deal with it.

Productivity peacocking is when you put more energy into looking busy than into doing meaningful work. Think replying to messages instantly instead of finishing the task at hand, or reorganizing your to-do list for the third time instead of crossing items off.

There's no single best time of day to work, since it depends on your body clock and when your energy naturally rises. Instead of trying to follow someone else's schedule, notice when you feel most alert, and dedicate that window to your most demanding work.

Yes, it's possible to be more productive without working longer hours, since a lot of time gets lost to switching tasks and reacting to interruptions. Try protecting focused blocks, sticking to one task at a time, and taking proper breaks, since a tired brain works slowly and rest can help you get more done.

Stress affects productivity by making it harder to focus, plan, and think clearly. When you're stressed, your brain pulls resources away from the areas that handle focus and memory. Bring your stress down and calm your mind with a few minutes of slow breathing.

One of the most effective ways to stop getting distracted while working is to remove the distraction before you start. Silence notifications, close the extra tabs, and place your phone out of reach so you're not relying on willpower in the moment. When your mind wanders anyway, and it will, bring it back without giving yourself a hard time.

Yes, meditation can help you be more productive, though the effect is indirect. In one randomized study, a two-week mindfulness course improved people's working memory and reduced how often their minds wandered mid-task.

You don't need long sessions, and even a few minutes a day of focusing your attention on your breath works the same mental muscle you use to stay on track while working.

#9554. What is languishing? Meaning, signs, and how to cope

Clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, MBA

Mental health struggles aren’t always obvious to the people experiencing them. Sometimes, you might just feel… stuck. You’re not exactly sad, but you’re not happy either. You’re not falling apart, but you’re definitely not thriving. That feeling is called languishing, and it’s more common than you think.

Basically, languishing is the state of mind between depression and flourishing. It’s that foggy middle ground where life feels muted.

And while languishing might not seem like a big deal, if you ignore it, it can quietly erode your sense of joy and purpose. That’s why it’s so important to understand what languishing is and explore ways to lift the fog and feel more connected to yourself again.

Languishing is the emotional equivalent of treading water. You’re not drowning, but you’re not moving forward either. You’re just floating, tired, and maybe even a little numb.

On the mental health spectrum, languishing falls somewhere between depression and flourishing — and it can come on so subtly that you don’t even realize it’s happening. If you’re languishing, you might struggle to concentrate or feel “meh” more days than not. You might not be able to remember the last time something excited you, or just have a general feeling of going through the motions without any real sense of meaning.

And because languishing doesn’t always feel like a problem that needs solving, it can be easy to ignore. Don’t. If it’s left unchecked, languishing can lead to deeper mental health challenges over time.

Languishing may seem similar to depression, burnout, and anxiety, but they’re different in key ways. Here’s how:

Depression: Depression is usually deeper and heavier than languishing. It can include persistent sadness, hopelessness, and a loss of pleasure in everything. You may also feel disconnected from yourself or others in a way that requires clinical care.

Burnout: Typically, burnout comes from chronic stress. It leads to emotional exhaustion, cynicism, and a sense of being overwhelmed. Languishing can overlap with burnout, but it’s usually broader, affecting your energy in all areas of life.

Anxiety: Anxiety is often high-energy and fear-based. It can show up as worry, racing thoughts, or a sense of dread. On the other hand, languishing feels flat.

Languishing can slowly build, dulling your emotional energy. Here are some reasons why it happens:

Chronic stress: Nonstop work pressure or caregiving can wear down your nervous system.

Disconnection: Not feeling connected to meaning can make your life feel empty or purposeless.

Prolonged uncertainty: Global unrest or personal instability can leave you emotionally worn out.

Lack of novelty: Doing the same thing day after day can cause your brain to check out from boredom.

Isolation: Lack of meaningful interactions can make you feel unseen or untethered.

If you’ve been feeling off without knowing why, you could be experiencing languishing. Here are five signs:

You’re coasting: You’re showing up and ticking boxes, but it all feels mechanical. You feel disconnected from any real sense of drive or direction.

Flow feels out of reach: Things you used to lose yourself in, like reading, creating, laughing, and dancing, have lost their appeal. You’re finding it hard to immerse yourself in anything, no matter how meaningful it once felt.

Your motivation has disappeared: Small plans you used to get excited about—like a weekend walk or trying a new recipe—now feel like uphill climbs. It takes more effort, and there’s less satisfaction.

Your emotions feel muted: You’re not experiencing intense sadness necessarily, but you’re also not feeling much else. It’s also harder to feel joy and excitement when things are going well.

Time feels strange: Days feel like they blend together, and you feel like you’re in a fog.

Languishing can make it hard to change things up and rebuild. But all change, no matter how big or small, starts with just one step. That’s all you have to do — one teeny step at a time.

Here are 10 small but meaningful ways to slowly begin moving forward.

Saying “I think I’m languishing” can bring a surprising sense of relief. It creates space between you and the experience.

It tells you that you’re not lazy, broken, or dramatic. You’re just in a tough emotional patch. Naming it gives you power, and it reminds you that this is a state, not a character flaw.

Read more: 10 mindfulness questions to help you check in with yourself

When you’re languishing, trying to feel great can backfire. Your goal should be to reconnect with anything that feels nourishing—like a song or a hot shower—not to feel endlessly inspired.

Start with where you are and slowly shift your internal goalposts from “thriving” to “engaged enough to care again.”

Here are 10 ways to reconnect with yourself if you’re feeling off right now.

Flow is that magical zone where you’re so absorbed in something that time disappears. You don’t have to lose hours. Just five to 10 minutes of doing something immersive can help to light you up again.

Try cooking a familiar recipe while listening to music or watering your plants, and notice how they’ve changed. You could also play a game on your phone that feels satisfying.

💙 Listening to Flow with Tamara Levitt can help you find yours.

Rigid routines can feel impossible when you’re low on energy, but a little structure helps.

Anchoring yourself with a morning stretch, a mid-day walk around the block, or a journaling session before bed might be just what you need to start feeling more like yourself.

Read more: 6 best morning stretches to wake up & start the day right

We tend to isolate when we’re languishing, but connection, even in tiny doses, can be one of the most effective antidotes. Consider sending a “thinking of you” message to someone you love or exchanging a friendly “hello” with your local barista.

Refocusing your attention can make you feel more centered.

Try turning off your phone while you eat a meal, reading a book for 10 minutes straight, or even concentrating on one movie instead of flipping between shows.

Get back into a hobby, a place, or a type of music you used to love. It may not be inspiring right away, and that’s okay. Many times, the action leads to the emotion.

Simple, restorative movement can help shift your mental energy, even subtly.

Try stretching in bed before you get up, doing a few yoga poses, or just taking your next phone call while standing.

💙 Get your blood pumping during this Mindful Movement session with Mel Mah.

Good enough is fine. Eat the frozen meal, ignore the dishes, or wear the same sweatshirt two days in a row. You don’t have to be impressive. You just have to be kind to yourself. Here are 10 ways to cultivate more self-kindness in your life.

You’re allowed not to be okay. If that’s the case, consider reaching out to a professional to see if they can help you get to the root cause of your emotions.

If asking for help feels too hard, try reaching out to a trusted friend. You could simply start by saying, “Hey, I’m not doing great. Can we talk soon?” or “I’m feeling off lately, and I just need someone to listen.”

Tiredness typically has a clear cause—like maybe you didn’t sleep well—and once you rest, the tiredness goes away. On the other hand, languishing persists even after you get some sleep or take time off.

Unlike simple exhaustion, languishing is an emotional and mental dullness that makes everything feel like a chore. If you’re waking up after a full night’s rest and still feeling apathetic or disconnected, you could be languishing.

There isn’t an official test for languishing, because it isn’t a clinical diagnosis. Researchers use a 14-question survey, developed by sociologist Corey Keyes, to sort people into languishing, moderate, or flourishing mental health. It’s built for research, so it can’t diagnose you.

Have most days felt flat or foggy for weeks?

Is it hard to feel interested in things you used to enjoy?

Does the feeling stay even after you rest?

If you said yes to several, you may be languishing. If you’re unsure, a doctor or mental health professional can help.

Languishing isn’t a clinical diagnosis, but that doesn’t mean it’s not real or important. Languishing is what psychologists call a “subclinical” state. This means that it doesn’t meet the criteria for mental illness, but it’s still a sign that your mental health needs attention.

Languishing is your brain’s version of a check engine light. It’s telling you that something’s off.

Languishing and depression can feel alike, so look at how heavy the feeling is and how it affects your days. When you’re languishing, you can usually keep up with daily life, but everything feels flat or foggy.

Depression goes deeper. It often brings hopelessness or feelings of worthlessness, and it can make daily tasks like working or sleeping hard.

If your mood is getting heavier, hasn’t lifted in several weeks, or you feel hopeless, talk to a doctor or mental health professional. If you can’t tell which one you’re dealing with, that’s reason enough to ask. Mindfulness can help with languishing, but it’s not a replacement for care.

Languishing isn’t another word for an existential crisis, but they can overlap. An existential crisis usually involves questioning the meaning of life, your purpose, or your place in the world. It tends to be philosophical and emotionally intense.

On the other hand, languishing is more like emotional white noise. Instead of asking, “What’s the point of it all?” You tend to ask,  “Why don’t I care about anything right now?”

That said, languishing can often trigger bigger questions about meaning and direction, especially if it lingers.

Languishing can last anywhere from a few weeks to several months, depending on your circumstances and support system. Sometimes it can fade on its own, especially if your environment changes or if you start naturally reconnecting with things that bring you energy. But often, it sticks around until you intervene.

If you’d like to stop feeling this way, small shifts in connection, movement, attention, and routine can start to turn the tide. The key is to treat it seriously, even if it feels subtle, because you deserve to feel alive again.

#9553. Does ADHD Worsen With Age? It Depends.

Whether ADHD worsens or improves over time for someone depends on multiple factors, from when symptoms and impairments first became meaningful to how sensitive one’s ADHD is to their environment.

Not too long ago, ADHD was largely thought of as a childhood condition that diminished in adulthood. Today, we understand that ADHD is a lifelong condition. What’s less clear: How does ADHD change across the lifespan, if at all?

This is a question that professor and clinical psychologist Margaret Sibley, Ph.D., addressed during her ADDitude webinar, “How ADHD Symptoms & Impairments Change with Age.”

The answer is still coming into focus but one central truth is emerging: There isn’t a single ADHD experience. Whether ADHD worsens or improves over time for someone depends on multiple factors, from when symptoms and impairments first become meaningful to how sensitive the individual’s ADHD is to their environment.

Sibley’s take-home from the research? “It depends on who you are.”

The question of how ADHD changes over time — whether it gets better or worse for people — is tricky, in part, because of the symptom vs. impairment question. That is, someone may show symptoms of ADHD, but the degree to which those symptoms impact their life may shift with age, overall health, and myriad other circumstances.

[Your Free Guide to ADHD in Older Adults]

“Not everyone who has symptoms is impaired,” Sibley said.

From major life transitions (like perimenopause and its accompanying impacts on cognition), environmental demands (e.g., a job that strains executive functioning) to coping skills, what’s going on in someone’s life “may influence whether a person actually experiences problems because of their symptoms,” Sibley said.

The question of whether ADHD worsens or improves over time suggests that the condition is linear. For many people, this is not the case.

“It doesn’t get better or get worse. But depending on what’s happening in your life, you may have good years and not-good years,” Sibley said, whose research found that higher environmental demands are associated with “better-functioning ADHD.”

[Read: ADHD’s Vanishing and Reappearing Act]

If you’ve experienced symptoms and impairments since childhood, your symptoms will likely get better, while impairments may or may not worsen.

If your symptoms first began to impact you in adulthood — perhaps triggered by aging, hormonal fluctuations, or other changes — research suggests that your symptoms and impairments may worsen over time.

If you’re part of the subgroup of people whose ADHD fluctuates from year to year, you may have a form of ADHD that is environmentally sensitive.

#9552. Where is the best place to meditate? Here’s how to find your spot

Clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, MBA

You have a free morning and want to meditate, but you’re not sure where. The living room isn’t private or quiet enough. The lighting in your home office is harsh. In your bedroom, the only place to sit is your bed, and you’re worried you might fall asleep. So instead of practicing mindfulness, you end up weighing the risks of distraction or discomfort.

The good news is, you don't need a Pinterest-worthy space, just a spot that works for you. People practice on train platforms, in parked cars, and on office floors during their lunch break, and they still get the benefits.

Whether you're just getting started or you’ve been meditating for years, this guide will help you find and level up that spot.

A good meditation space is one where you feel safe, comfortable, and undisturbed. These four qualities tend to make the biggest difference:

Comfort: A supportive cushion, a chair with a good backrest, or even a spot against the wall reduces strain on your body.

Quiet: Minimal noise, foot traffic, or notifications helps you avoid competition for your attention.

Calming sensory cues: Soft lamplight, a candle, a diffuser, or a warm blanket can signal it’s time to slow down.

Familiarity: The same corner or cushion becomes a cue over time, so your brain starts to wind down as soon as you arrive.

💙 Just starting out? Here’s a detailed guide on how to meditate for beginners.

The best place to meditate depends on what you want from your session, and many people rotate between a few spots. Indoors is more predictable, since weather and temperature are rarely a factor. Outdoors, on the other hand, can feel more grounding and restorative.

When you meditate indoors, you have more control over the temperature, lighting, and setup of the space, which can help you build a consistent habit.

Your bedroom corner. It's private and may already feel like a place to recharge, so it works well when you want to slow down.

Your living room. This spot works best when it’s empty, like early morning before anyone's up or once the house has gone quiet for the night.

Your unused nook or closet. With just a cushion and a curtain, almost any small, overlooked area can become your own little sanctuary.

Your bed. Meditating here is a gentle way to start your day or transition into sleep, though the same comfort that makes it appealing can also make you doze off before you're done.

💙 For ways to turn any of these spots into a dedicated space, see Calm's meditation room ideas.

💙 For more on the bed option specifically, check out bedtime meditation techniques.

The outdoors offers something special: fresh air, the open sky, and nature sounds that help calm your nervous system. Time in green space is linked to lower cortisol and reduced stress. One explanation is the attention restoration theory — the idea that natural settings give your focus a chance to recover.

A backyard or garden. If you have one, some greenery and a comfortable seat can turn it into a peaceful retreat.

A beach or park. Either works especially well near water, where the sound of waves or a stream can ease your mind.

A balcony or patch of grass. Even a small outdoor space gives you a change of scenery, which can help you relax.

💙 For more on practicing outside, see Calm’s guides on outdoor meditation and building a meditation garden.

If sitting feels hard, try walking meditation. Focus on the rhythm of your steps to give your mind something to settle on.

A few small, deliberate changes can turn your meditation space into one that genuinely supports your practice.

Store your cushion, blanket, and anything else you use to meditate in your dedicated place. When you return to the same spot consistently, ideally around the same time, settling in can start to feel automatic.

Face away from clutter, toward a blank wall or window. In a shared space, a folding screen or blanket draped over a chair can mark off your corner. Even with your eyes closed, feeling tucked away can help you settle.

Try playing steady background noise—like soothing nature sounds or music—to cover unpredictable and intrusive sounds like traffic or a neighbor's TV. If you prefer some structure in your practice, you could follow a guided meditation.

To slow down, experiment with tracks around 60–80 beats per minute, which researchers have linked to a slower heart rate. For daytime focus, many people find that ambient or instrumental sound works best.

💙 Calm's guides on meditation music can help you find what fits your needs.

Put your phone on Do Not Disturb, and tell the people you live with that you'll be unavailable for the length of your session. You could also pick a time when they’re less likely to need you.

💙 Try the Single-Tasking session with Jay Shetty on Calm.

If you need to take the strain off your lower back, sit on a cushion or folded blanket to raise your hips slightly above your knees. You can also meditate near a wall, or place a chair nearby to support your spine if sitting upright gets tiring.

A meditation cushion can help you hold your position more comfortably. Try keeping the room on the cool side too, since an overly warm setup can nudge you toward sleep.

💙 Explore the Posture session from the 7 Days of Calm series.

💙 Learn about the different meditation postures to find the right fit for you.

Where you meditate shapes how the practice feels once you're there, but consistency is what matters most. A pleasant space can motivate you to start, though it's not required.

You can still meditate in a noisy home or busy neighborhood, and plenty of people do. Headphones with a guided session or ambient sound can add a bit of calm almost anywhere, even a parked car or a bathroom.

You can even let the noise become part of the practice by resting your attention on the sounds themselves, instead of trying to push them away. Over time, that flexibility often makes your practice stronger.

You don’t need much to set up a meditation corner. A cushion, a clear patch of floor, and some calming objects are enough. Pick an empty corner and mark it off with a plant, a small rug, or a curtain.

Meditating in bed is fine, and it's a gentle way to wind down at night or start your morning. If you’re worried about dozing off, sit up against the headboard instead of lying down, or try it earlier in the day when you’re more alert.

To reduce distractions when you meditate, start with what you can control: silence your phone and pick a time when interruptions are less likely.

For noises that still come up, treat your breath as your anchor and return to it whenever your mind wanders.

💙 Calm's guides on what to focus on during meditation and how to improve focus go deeper on taming a wandering mind.

Your meditation space doesn't need to look a certain way. It just needs to work for you. Soft light, minimal clutter, and something comfortable to sit on are usually enough.

Music and calming sounds can ease you into your meditation. Soft instrumental tracks, nature sounds, or steady background noise all help mask distracting noises and signal to your body that it’s time to relax.

As your practice develops, you might find you prefer silence, so it's worth experimenting to see what suits you.

#9551. How to Deal With the Grief of an Aging Body

Become a subscribing member today. Help us continue to bring “the science of a meaningful life” to you and to millions around the globe.

Greater Good Science Center • Magazine • In Action • In Education

Body changes can raise disturbing feelings, such as looking in a mirror and seeing a reflection that may feel spiritually empty, unproductive, ugly, or weak.

Unpleasant sensations such as pain, pins and needles, soreness coursing through limbs, and an inexplicable fog filling the head are a reminder that this body is not the same you anymore, prompting us to wish there was a way to get back there. It may feel impossible to live well unless you do.

This is the disillusionment that most of the population will face at some point in life, through aging, chronic pain, or invisible illness (a disease or health problem that cannot be externally seen, including autoimmune diseases, chronic pain and fatigue, and recently, long COVID).

Recent global estimates suggest one in five people are currently experiencing chronic pain. The most prevalent chronic pain reported by adults ages 75 and over includes low back pain and migraine, while tension-type headaches are more often experienced by younger adults. Chronic illness (diabetes, heart disease, and other mid-to-late-life diagnoses) affects about three-quarters of the world population.

Despite how common chronic illness is worldwide, the nuances of navigating a changing body are not often discussed. It’s time for an honest, evidence-based conversation about what it means to navigate chronic pain and illness, aging and transforming identity post-diagnosis, and how to grieve this loss and maintain meaning through these changes.

Research suggest that those with internalized stigma of chronic illness are more preoccupied with how their illness detracts from their view of themselves, and also have a greater tendency to overlook positive aspects of life with a chronic illness.

Psychologists have observed how preoccupation with illness or pain is often accompanied by other grief behaviors. A 2025 study explored how Danish chronic illness patients navigated loss and growth. The study found that many with chronic illness find themselves mourning the life that they thought they would have, often leading to loss of motivation and joy in everyday life.

The perception of losing the life they had once envisioned is often accompanied by a focus on getting back to the “before illness” version of themselves as people struggle to accept how their body has changed, perhaps in how it looks but definitely in how it feels.

These changes and associated feelings of loss often permeate a person’s sense of identity, as well as their perceived roles within social relationships. Many report a fear of burdening others, especially loved ones, often describing feelings of guilt that “others have it worse than I do.” This is where internalized stigma festers.

Some people have also described feelings of anger, isolation, shame, and exhaustion accompanying sadness. Meanwhile, others have expressed frustration over a gradual loss rather than a “clean break,” accompanied by the inability to find closure.

First, it’s important to understand why accepting this continuous loss feels so impossible. Theories of control in psychology state that humans desire control or the ability to achieve a desired outcome according to our own standards.

The best and most enduring of our articles, podcasts, and videos about getting older.

When that ability is seen as stripped away, people are more likely to experience negative mental health symptoms, like anxiety, depression, and even grief. Specifically, feelings of diminished perceived control (subjective belief about our ability to achieve desired outcomes) occur when we face continuous roadblocks to living our desired life because of chronic illness.

One of the major consequences of loss and major life change is that it can disrupt meaning and challenge identity, purpose, and assumptions about the future. At a time when people feel there is little they can control, psychologist Robert Neimeyer’s Meaning Reconstruction Theory poses the questions: “How do I move forward?” and “What matters most?”

While the original theory was proposed as an approach to coping with the loss of a loved one, the process is somewhat similar to grieving the close ally that is your body. This theory approaches grief by making sense of the loss and finding ways to rebuild a sense of purpose in a changed life (and body).

To answer relevant questions about how to move forward with chronic illness, two ongoing approaches are needed: integrating the loss and recentering purpose and meaning.

Integrating the loss may look like processing significant bodily losses in therapy, finding trusted loved ones to talk about the loss with, and focusing on being realistic about your current body without judgment.

Second, recentering purpose during this major life change involves understanding your why: why is this loss so significant to you, why does it hurt? Maybe it’s because you love hiking in the mountains and a new diagnosis with arthritis feels like the end of this joy. Part of rebuilding meaning is finding new approaches to fulfilling this purpose—perhaps hiking may look different, but nature can be accessed and loved with chronic illness present.

Rebuilding meaning might also look like making meaning from this loss: What has this change taught you about yourself, about the impact you can make? Approaching present and future with this perspective helps process grief in a more protective way.

Living with chronic pain, illness, and the changes that come with aging often involves grieving physical loss, but also shifts in purpose, relationships, identity, and future plans. While these changes challenge our perceived control and purpose, the Meaning Reconstruction Theory suggests that acceptance and growth comes with integrating loss and rebuilding purpose alongside these changes.

Although the present is different than anticipated, fulfillment is still possible with your current body.

This article is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons license. Read the original article.

Li-elle Rapaport is a doctoral candidate in clinical psychology and a supervised therapist. Her clinical work is informed by evidence-based approaches, including Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT) and Mindful Self-Compassion, and her doctoral research focuses on aging and mental health.

When Lisa Kwon lost someone dear to her, she found meaning and comfort in playing Pokémon Pokopia.

We talk with neuroscientist Antonio Damasio about the science of consciousness, how it works in the body, and how it aims to keep us alive.

You can be good at your job and still feel a lack of engagement, challenge, and meaning.

What does it actually take to put people over politics? Republican and Democrat students discover ways to resist the pull to demean or villainize people with whom they strongly disagree.

This guided meditation with end-of-life doula Andrea Sexton-Dumas offers a gentle way to make space for grief by imagining sharing your heartache with a plant, releasing it into the soil, and nurturing the earth that holds it.

#9550. Two Personality Traits Linked To A Sharper Mind

How you respond to beauty may have more in common with your thinking skills than you realise.

How you respond to beauty may have more in common with your thinking skills than you realise.

Intellectual curiosity and an appreciation of beauty are both linked to stronger thinking skills.

People with these qualities tend to perform better on tests of literacy, numeracy and problem-solving.

The findings suggest that a person’s interest in ideas and aesthetic experiences may offer clues to their cognitive abilities.

Curiosity could encourage people to seek out opportunities to learn, while stronger thinking skills could make exploring complex ideas more rewarding, with both processes reinforcing one another.

Intellectual curiosity involves enjoying ideas, wanting to understand things and being drawn to questions that require thought.

Aesthetic sensitivity describes an appreciation of art and beauty.

Both qualities belong to the broader personality trait of openness to experience, which captures how receptive people are to unfamiliar ideas and experiences.

However, openness also includes creative imagination, and this aspect showed no significant independent association with cognitive performance.

Imagination, curiosity and an appreciation of beauty may overlap in everyday life, but their relationships with thinking skills differ.

The conclusions come from an analysis of almost 68,000 people across 12 countries, including Canada, Germany, Italy and New Zealand.

They completed personality questionnaires alongside assessments of literacy, numeracy and the ability to solve problems as circumstances change.

Intellectual curiosity and aesthetic sensitivity were linked to better performance across all three assessments, even after accounting for other personality traits.

The connections between personality and cognitive skills also varied between countries.

Educational systems and cultural practices could help explain such differences, although the reasons remain uncertain.

Overall, the findings link both a desire to understand the world and an appreciation of its beauty with stronger thinking skills.

The study was published in the journal Large-scale Assessments in Education (Rammstedt et al., 2026).

Psychologist, Jeremy Dean, PhD is the founder and author of PsyBlog. He holds a doctorate in psychology from University College London and two other advanced degrees in psychology. He has been writing about scientific research on PsyBlog since 2004. View all posts by Dr Jeremy Dean

#9549. Challenges mounting to US laws enacted to aid recovery of Nazi-looted art

Camille Pissarro's Rue Saint-Honoré, dans l'après-midi. Effet de pluie (1897), at the Museo Nacional Thyssen-Bornemisza in Madrid, has been the subject of a Nazi-loot restitution claim in California for decades Photo © The Art Newspaper

Reopened claims in California are testing new laws that were enacted to counteract court decisions in favour of museums in Nazi-looted art cases. The California and US federal statutes, which change the procedural rules for Nazi-looted art claims, are being challenged by the Thyssen-Bornemisza Collection Foundation (TBCF) in Madrid, and the Norton Simon Museum (NSM) in Pasadena, California.

Both museums are facing new litigation in art ownership claims that were previously decided in their favour by court judgments which both Congress and the California legislature cited negatively as reasons for changing the law. The challenges by the museum and foundation now launch the statutes towards court judgment themselves as to their permissibility.

On 19 October, Judge John Walter of the federal district court in Los Angeles said he would issue a decision in the TBCF case without oral argument, based on the submitted briefs. The museum and plaintiffs have each moved for summary judgment in the reconsideration of a claim to recover a Nazi-looted painting by Camille Pissarro, which had already been adjudicated in favour of TBCF.

The reconsideration was ordered in 2025 by the US Supreme Court, after California amended its procedural laws in 2024 to aid state residents who sue museums for stolen works of art. The legislature criticised a 2022 Ninth Circuit federal court of appeals decision which said Spanish property law applied to the TBCF case, and that under the Spanish “acquisitive prescription” principle, TBCF owned the painting. The work is Pissarro’s Rue Saint Honoré, apres midi, effect de pluie (1897). The Supreme Court vacated the decision because under California’s new procedural statute, California’s substantive law, and no one else’s, applies in claims for stolen art at museums, regardless of prior judicial decisions.

The plaintiffs, David Cassirer and other heirs of the original owner, Lilly Neubauer, justify recovery of the painting because Neubauer, a Jew based in Berlin, was forced in 1939 to sell it to Nazis to obtain an exit visa, and was not allowed to access the payment. In the renewed proceedings, Neubauer’s heirs argue that under the new California rule, California’s property law applies, “under which good title can never be acquired to stolen property”. The painting therefore must be returned to them as rightful owners. The plaintiffs also cite a second legislative change, which followed soon after California’s: the amendment by the US Congress of the federal Holocaust Era Art Recovery (Hear) Act. The amendment took effect in April 2026 and was expressly applicable to pending lawsuits.

For Nazi-loot claims that it covers, the new Hear Act bars art possessors from relying on “defences or substantive doctrines based on the passage of time”, including “acquisitive prescription”. The prior court proceedings had found that TBCF earned ownership of the painting under Spanish acquisitive prescription, because TBCF possessed the painting for more than six years without actually knowing it was stolen. The plaintiffs say that the 2025 Hear Act’s bar of any reliance on acquisitive prescription thus “conclusively resolves” all issues in their favour.

But the TBCF is challenging the new statutes. It says that the California law violates the US constitution by retroactively denying it of its vested property rights in the painting without due process, and that the Hear Act, if applied to this case to achieve that, will be unconstitutional too. Acquisitive prescription is not a “defence based on the passage of time”, but a property vesting law under the substantive law of Spain, it says, and prior court decisions in the case repeatedly found that TBCF’s property rights vested no later than 1999, “more than twenty-six years before the [Hear] Act’s enactment”. The TBCF makes multiple other challenges to the new laws, including that the new California law is an impermissible state attempt to regulate conduct extraterritorially in Spain.

The governments of the United States and California have intervened in the lawsuit, submitting briefs defending the constitutionality of their statutes. Friend of the court briefs have also been filed on both sides. A decision is expected likely by late February.

ucas Cranach the Elder, Adam and Eve (around 1530)

In the second lawsuit, the NSM on 14 October challenged a complaint filed in September in state court and removed it to the federal district court in Los Angeles. The claimants seek recovery of a diptych, Adam and Eve (around 1530), by Lucas Cranach the Elder. The paintings were among 800 works stolen from the Old Masters dealership in the Netherlands owned by Jacques Goudstikker, a Dutch Jew, by Nazi Reichsmarschall Hermann Göring in 1940.

Prior litigation seeking the Cranach diptych ended in a judgment for the museum. In 2018, the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals dismissed the case based on the “act of state” doctrine, under which the actions of the Dutch government within its borders, including its allegedly wrongful sale of the Cranach paintings to a third party, cannot be adjudicated by US courts. The prior litigation was brought by Marei von Saher, Goudstikker’s sole surviving heir.

The current lawsuit relies on the new California law allowing new claims even if previously dismissed on procedural grounds, and is brought by Von Saher’s assignees, Daniel Gryczman and the Jewish Federation Council of Greater Los Angeles. The NSM is telling the court that the new lawsuit is a “misguided and meritless” action seeking to relieve the museum from its prior judgment, and is requesting a permanent injunction precluding the re-litigation. The prior judgment dismissed Von Saher’s claims “on the merits” andquieted NSM’s title to the Cranach diptych, the museum’s representatives say, and it asks the court to grant its requests to spare it “the open-ended threat of future litigation”.

A third lawsuit is also unfolding based on the new California law. In it, the daughters of the Czech Jewish artist Dina Gottliebova Babbitt are seeking recovery from the Auschwitz-Birkenau State Museum (ABM) in Poland of portraits Babbitt was forced to create while imprisoned at the Auschwitz-Birkenau concentration camp. Under the process required to sue a foreign government instrumentality, the museum, an instrumentality of Poland, has not yet been joined to the case, a representative for the ABM tells The Art Newspaper, and has not yet filed a response. Babbitt’s daughters filed their complaint in September.

The Hear Act amendment is also being tested in other federal courts. One of the cases, brought against Austria and two Austrian museums in the federal district court for the Southern District of New York, is considering the constitutionality of the Hear Act’s denial of otherwise applicable defences.

The Supreme Court’s order requires the decades-long dispute over a painting at the Museo Nacional Thyssen-Bornemisza in Madrid to be re-examined in light of a new California statute

Lawsuits related to a Cranach diptych at the Norton Simon Museum of Art and a group of watercolours at the Auschwitz-Birkenau State Museum were filed two days before a 2024 California statute expired

The new law signed by Governor Gavin Newsom is intended to resolve a decades-long restitution claim in a California family’s favour

The latest chapter in the 20-year dispute over a painting currently in the collection of a Madrid museum suggests the case may head back to a California appeals court

#9548. How ADHD Science Fails Women in Menopause

Menopause worsens ADHD symptoms, but standard assessments do not capture the depth of women’s misery.

Menopause aggravates and elevates ADHD symptoms for a staggering 97.5 percent of women with the condition, according to a survey of 600 women cited in the Journal of Psychiatric Research.1 Complaints include increased difficulty with attention, emotional regulation, and managing everyday demands – symptoms that significantly degrade quality of life yet remain largely unaddressed in midlife ADHD treatment plans.

The Adult ADHD Self-Report Scale (ASRS) – one of the standard measures for assessing common ADHD symptoms – may not fully capture how much menopause interferes with daily life because it was not specifically designed to measure changes in ADHD across hormonal transitions.

While nearly all of the 600 women in the survey reported worsening ADHD symptoms during menopause, their ASRS scores were similar across different hormonal life stages. This apparent contradiction deserves attention. A woman may experience a major change in mental clarity, working memory, motivation, emotional regulation, and managing day-to-day responsibilities without necessarily showing a large change on a standard ADHD symptom checklist.

[Get This Free Download: Menopause and ADHD]

This points to a critical need for better ways to assess ADHD across the lifespan and to understand how hormonal changes may alter its presentation and impact.

Today, we know about ADHD in menopause thanks, largely, to women’s personal accounts. Though surveys and self-reports cannot establish cause and effect in the same way as controlled clinical trials, they are an essential starting point. They can identify patterns and raise questions that researchers need to investigate.

One central question is regarding the safety and efficacy of prescribing hormone replacement therapy (HRT) and/or ADHD medication to women in perimenopause and menopause. Sadly, evidence specifically supporting combined HRT and stimulant treatment remains limited. We need well-designed studies to determine which women might benefit, what treatments are most effective, and how the medications may interact.

[Read: How Hormonal Changes Impact ADHD Symptoms in Women]

The voices of women with ADHD have brought this issue into view. Now clinicians and researchers have an opportunity – and a responsibility – to listen carefully, investigate rigorously, and translate emerging knowledge into better care.

Kathleen Nadeau, Ph.D., is the founder and clinical director of the Institute for Lifespan ADHD Training.

#9547. Do you have a fear of leaving the house? How to cope with agoraphobia

Clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, MBA

Some days, even the thought of stepping outside can make your chest tighten. The world feels too big, too unpredictable, and your home feels like the only place that's safe. This experience is more common than most people realize, and it often points to something called agoraphobia, or the fear of leaving the house.

People who experience agoraphobia aren't necessarily weak, but rather trying to create safety and control in their day-to-day experience. This particular phobia can stem from intense experiences like trauma, but can also be rooted in genetics and lived experience. While there's nothing wrong with wanting to feel safe at home, agoraphobia can make everyday tasks like running errands or going to work feel daunting and overwhelming.

Learning to ease back into exploring the world at large can help make life feel more… well, livable. So, let's explore what causes agoraphobia, what can make it worse, and a few evidence-based ways to start rebuilding a sense of ease in the world and the return of your freedom.

Agoraphobia often starts with a negative experience. A panic attack on the subway, a dizzy spell in a grocery store, a sudden wave of fear that seems to come from nowhere. When that happens, the body remembers and starts building invisible boundaries to prevent it from happening again. What starts as caution can slowly turn into avoidance, until even ordinary outings feel overwhelming.

Clinically, agoraphobia is often linked to anxiety or panic disorders, though it can develop on its own. The fear isn't about the world itself, but about losing control or facing uncomfortable sensations in public. If you've ever thought, “What if I panic and can't escape?” that's the loop agoraphobia reinforces. And your brain's attempt to protect you ends up feeding the fear.

Past panic attacks or trauma: Experiences that felt unsafe or uncontrollable can leave the body on high alert long after the danger has passed.

Chronic stress or burnout: When your nervous system is constantly under strain, it becomes more reactive to triggers.

Family history or genetics: Anxiety disorders can run in families, likely due to a mix of inherited traits and learned coping patterns.

Personality and temperament: People who tend to be more sensitive, cautious, or introspective may notice and internalize physical sensations more deeply, which can heighten fear responses.

Other mental health conditions: Depression, social anxiety, and PTSD can all overlap with or contribute to agoraphobic symptoms.

Read more: What are the most common phobias? Plus, how to treat them

Agoraphobia doesn't always look the same for everyone. For some, it's a strong hesitation to go far from home. For others, it means avoiding specific situations where escape might feel difficult or embarrassing, like crowded stores, public transit, or open spaces. The fear isn't necessarily about the place itself, but about what might happen once you're there.

These symptoms can range from mild to severe and may come and go. You might still leave the house sometimes, but only under specific conditions, or you might find that even opening the door feels unbearable. Here are a few common symptoms:

Physical symptoms often overlap with panic or anxiety responses. You might notice:

A racing heartbeat, shortness of breath, or dizziness

Feeling detached from your surroundings or like you might faint

Chest tightness or a sense that something terrible is about to happen

Emotional and behavioral symptoms can develop as you try to avoid those sensations:

Relying on a friend or family member to accompany you outside

Feeling trapped, frustrated, or ashamed for not being able to “just go out”

Increased anxiety or depression from isolation

Triggers can vary widely, but they usually share one thing: they stir feelings of uncertainty or vulnerability. A crowded concert, a long commute, a sudden noise, or even imagining an unfamiliar situation can spark a fear response.

Crowded or enclosed spaces, like buses, malls, or elevators

Open or exposed places, such as parking lots or wide streets

Previous panic experiences, especially if they happened in public

Health anxiety, such as fearing a medical emergency far from home

Avoidance often feels like relief in the short term, but over time, it reinforces the fear. The brain learns that staying home equals safety, while leaving equals danger.

Agoraphobia can also worsen during periods of high stress or change. Even positive life events—like moving, starting a new job, or entering a relationship—can unsettle a nervous system already wired for hypervigilance.

Recovery focuses on gently retraining your body to tolerate fear without letting it dictate your choices. It's a gradual, compassionate process that rebuilds trust in the world beyond your walls.

Related read: What it actually means to “be triggered” (and how to cope)

When you're living with agoraphobia, recovery can be tricky. You don't want to force yourself to go outside if you don't feel safe. The idea is to build a sense of safety first, starting small and working up to leaving the house. These strategies are drawn from clinical research and real-world practice and are designed to help you move at your own pace while gently retraining your brain and body to trust the world again.

It’s important to remember that avoiding what scares you isn’t a sign of weakness; it’s your brain trying to protect you. Your nervous system probably learned that certain places or situations feel unsafe, so it tries to keep you away.

Agoraphobia sets off a real physiological fear response. When the brain senses threat, it switches on the nervous system's fight-or-flight mode, so your heart rate climbs, your breathing goes shallow, and your muscles tense. Knowing this takes some of the power out of it. You're not going crazy. Your brain is doing its job, in the wrong context.

Start by observing your fear with curiosity. Ask yourself, when does it appear? What sensations come first, what thoughts follow? This kind of mindful attention helps you separate real danger from false alarms. A short daily journal—just a few lines—can make it easier to spot patterns.

💙 If anxiety or panic catches you off guard, reach for Tamara Levitt's Panic SOS session on Calm to work with your breath and body when you need it most.

When panic or anxiety rises, grounding practices can help your body remember it’s safe right now. These techniques calm the stress response by reconnecting you with your senses.

If going outside feels overwhelming, start at home — by an open window or your doorway. Gradually, your body learns that calm is possible beyond your comfort zone.

💙 Try the 5-4-3-2-1 grounding technique on the Calm app.

Gradual exposure therapy—facing feared situations in small, structured steps—is one of the most evidence-based ways to ease agoraphobia. Start where your anxiety feels manageable, then increase the challenge as confidence grows.

Sit near your front door for a few minutes.

Visit a quiet store or café during off-hours.

The aim isn't to feel no anxiety. It's to stay in the situation long enough for anxiety to come down on its own, and to show yourself, again and again, that you can handle it. Each step helps your brain link “outside” with safety. Celebrate even the smallest wins. Progress may be uneven, but every step counts.

💙 Explore Ease Your Social Anxiety with Jeff Warren on Calm, designed to help your world expand again at your own pace.

Avoidance is the mechanism that keeps agoraphobia in place. Every time anxiety pushes you to cancel plans or stay home, and you give in, it reinforces the idea that the feared situation was dangerous. Over time, the list of “unsafe” places and situations tends to grow.

Noticing when avoidance is happening, and gently questioning it, is part of recovery. That doesn't mean forcing yourself into overwhelming situations. It means asking: is this decision based on actual risk, or on anxiety talking?

💙 Turn toward what you're avoiding rather than away from it with Emotions Series: Investigating Anxiety, led by John Armstrong on Calm.

A licensed therapist, especially one trained in cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) or exposure therapy, can help you challenge anxious thoughts and gradually expand your comfort zone.

If therapy feels intimidating, try starting with a telehealth session. Many people with agoraphobia begin remotely and move to in-person care later. Therapists can also teach tools like cognitive restructuring (questioning catastrophic thoughts) and interoceptive exposure (reducing fear of physical sensations).

If cost is a barrier, ask about low-cost or sliding-scale sessions.

Read more: How CBT can help calm your anxiety (and 5 ways to try it today)

Agoraphobia can feel isolating, but recovery is rarely something you do alone. Support from trusted friends, family, or peer groups can help you stay connected when your world feels small.

Identify one or two people who can listen without minimizing your fear. Be clear about what helps, like “Please don't push me to go out, but check in after I try.”

Online support communities for agoraphobia or panic disorder can also be powerful spaces to share progress and encouragement. Connection doesn't have to mean going far, just not going alone.

Related read: 7 tips on how to communicate your needs in a relationship

Your nervous system can't process new experiences if it's stuck in survival mode. Before trying exposure work, focus on calming your baseline stress.

Slow breathing (inhale 4 counts, exhale 6)

Limiting caffeine or alcohol if they spike anxiety

The longer exhale matters. It activates the parasympathetic nervous system, which helps the body downshift from a high-alert state. These habits won't "cure" agoraphobia, but they can give your body the steadiness it needs to face fear safely.

Mindfulness doesn't mean clearing your mind, but noticing thoughts and sensations without reacting to them. When you can observe fear rather than fight it, it starts to lose its grip.

Then focus on your breath or the feeling of your feet on the floor. You're not trying to make the fear vanish, just reminding yourself you can stay present while it passes. With practice, your brain can learn that fear doesn't always mean danger.

💙 Explore these Tools for Anxiety and Stress with Dr. Julie on the Calm app.

Progress with agoraphobia often feels like two steps forward, one step back. Some days you'll walk outside easily; others, just getting dressed takes effort. That's okay.

Set small, specific goals like opening a window, walking to the mailbox, or standing outside for 30 seconds. Track and celebrate each one. Speak to yourself as you would to a friend since compassion keeps recovery moving when motivation fades.

There will be days when something that felt manageable last week feels impossible again. That's not failure. It's a normal feature of recovering from an anxiety disorder. What matters is returning to your plan after a setback rather than writing off the progress you've made.

Mindfulness won't cure agoraphobia, but it can help you manage it. There's research that suggests mindfulness may reduce anxiety by helping people look at fearful thoughts and body sensations without getting swept up in them.

That matters with agoraphobia. Fear isn't just about the situation you're in. It also sets off a chain of anxious thoughts that make physical symptoms feel worse. Mindfulness helps you notice that chain without automatically following it.

Even five to ten minutes of meditation a day may help change how your brain responds to fear over time. It won't make anxiety go away, but it can make it easier to handle. For anyone who finds leaving home hard, a home-based app like Calm makes this practice easy to access without any extra pressure.

Read more: Mindfulness for beginners: 6 techniques for mindful living

Agoraphobia is treatable. With the right combination of therapy, support, and sometimes medication, many people reclaim a sense of calm and freedom they thought was lost.

Reaching out for help when you can barely leave the house can feel impossible. For many people with agoraphobia, even calling a therapist can trigger anxiety. But asking for help is simply a sign you're ready for support.

Consider professional help if your fear limits work, school, or relationships; if you feel trapped at the thought of leaving home; or if you depend on others to go out. When your world starts shrinking, or hopelessness sets in, it's time for extra care. Early treatment also tends to be more effective than waiting for symptoms to worsen, and it doesn't require hitting a low point first.

Curious to learn more about other phobias and how to treat them?  Having a deeper understanding of common phobias, like acrophobia or metathesiophobia, can help you get to know yourself better and give you tools for treating them or easing their symptoms.

The fear of leaving the house often develops after experiences that made you feel unsafe or out of control — like a panic attack in public, trauma, or chronic stress. Over time, your brain links "outside" with danger and "home" with safety.

Common signs include anxiety or panic outside the home, fear of crowds, public transport, or open and enclosed spaces, and a strong urge to avoid those situations. Some people can only manage them with someone else present. Physical symptoms can include a racing heart, dizziness, shortness of breath, and chest tightness. If this is limiting where you go or what you do, talk to a doctor or mental health professional.

Not always, but they often overlap. Agoraphobia is a clinical term for anxiety about situations where escape might be difficult or help unavailable during panic. The fear of leaving home can be one part of that pattern. Some people feel anxious in only a few situations, while others avoid most public places.

No, though they can overlap. Social anxiety is about fear of judgment from others. Agoraphobia is about fear of situations where escape feels difficult or panic might happen. Both involve avoidance, but the triggers are different and so are the treatment approaches.

Common triggers include crowded or open spaces, traveling alone, driving, public transit, or past experiences of panic. Emotional stress, health worries, or major life changes can also heighten symptoms.

Triggers are deeply personal; learning what sets off your fear is a key part of recovery, because it helps you prepare, plan, and respond with more calm.

Yes. Many people with agoraphobia still leave home but limit when, where, or how they do it — maybe only with a trusted companion or in familiar areas. Agoraphobia exists on a spectrum, and partial avoidance is common.

The goal of treatment isn’t to eliminate all fear, but to help you feel more confident and capable outside, even when anxiety shows up.

Start with very small steps and build gradually. Open the door and stand outside for a minute. Walk to the mailbox. Sit in your car. Over time, extend your distance or duration. Pair these moments with grounding techniques and self-compassion.

If fear or avoidance is getting in the way of work, relationships, or daily life, it's a good time to reach out. You don't need to be housebound to ask for help. A therapist who specializes in anxiety can offer structured treatment, including CBT and exposure work, that's hard to replicate on your own.

Agoraphobia recovery combines understanding, gradual exposure, nervous system regulation, and professional support. Grounding techniques, mindfulness, and therapy—especially cognitive behavioral or exposure therapy—can help retrain your fear response.

Compassion is essential; you’re learning to reintroduce safety to your body, not forcing yourself to be “brave.”

It varies. Some people see real improvement within a few months of consistent CBT and exposure work. Others take a year or more. Progress is usually gradual and setbacks are normal. How long it takes depends on severity, how long symptoms have been present, and access to treatment. Consistency matters more than speed.

Yes, when done properly. Good exposure therapy is gradual. It starts with situations that bring up mild anxiety and builds slowly from there. It should never mean being pushed into something overwhelming without preparation. Working with a trained therapist keeps the pace right and makes sure coping tools are in place before each step.

The most effective treatments are cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), exposure therapy, and sometimes medication like SSRIs or SNRIs. Teletherapy can also help if in-person sessions feel too difficult.

Many people benefit from combining approaches that balance science with emotional safety.

Yes, when used gently. Meditation can help calm the body’s stress response and increase awareness of anxious thoughts without getting caught in them.

However, for some people, sitting still with intense anxiety can feel overwhelming. Start small—guided breathing, body scans, or walking meditations—and use it as one tool among others, not a cure-all.

Recovery tends to reopen parts of life that anxiety had closed off: work, relationships, travel, and everyday spontaneity. Many people also notice a broader shift in confidence, and find they start attempting things they'd written off, not just outside the home, but in other areas where anxiety had been calling the shots.

Symptoms can lessen over time, especially with self-awareness and stress reduction, but full recovery usually requires intentional support. Without treatment, the avoidance cycle can deepen.

The good news is that with therapy and consistent practice, many people regain independence and confidence, even after years of fear.

#9545. Calm launches Shift to help people feel better in the moment through sound

Shift is a new dedicated in-app experience designed to help people relieve stress, wind down, focus, and feel better through bilateral audio, an audio-based approach inspired by a technique therapists use that moves sound intentionally between your ears.

Shift offers four states to move into, grounded in everyday needs: Focus, Release, Uplift, and Sleep, each through its own custom bilateral track. It also includes a 7-day guided program and 20+ additional tracks to browse, including an exclusive track from popular duo, Daisy the Great.

Shift is one of Calm's largest expansions into a category since Sleep Stories, following increased user and cultural demand since it began developing this content in 2022.

SAN FRANCISCO, CA – October 27, 2026 – Calm, a trusted leader in mental wellness with the #1 app to help you sleep more, stress less and live mindfully, launches Shift – a new in-app offering designed to help people shift how they feel in the moment using bilateral audio, an audio-based approach inspired by a technique therapists use. At launch, Shift provides a 7-day guided program and more than 20 custom bilateral tracks, including an exclusive song by popular New York-based duo, Daisy the Great.

Bilateral audio intentionally moves sound between the left and right ear, creating a natural rhythm designed to help shift your mood, whether that’s finally settling into sleep, releasing the day’s tension, or clearing afternoon fog. No special skills required, just headphones and a few minutes.

Calm added bilateral audio content to its music library in 2022 and has since seen user and cultural demand build. It’s one of the top search terms on Calm, Google search for “bilateral audio” is up over 5000% in the past year, and across the internet, concepts like “brain flossing” have gone viral, pointing to bilateral stimulation to “clear mental clutter”.

“Calm’s origins are rooted in making meditation accessible, but we never intended to be a meditation-only app,” said Dun Wang, CEO of Calm. “We want to be a place people can come to feel better, in whatever way they need. At first it was meditation, then it was sleep, which led to the launch of Sleep Stories, an innovative format that is now one of our most popular offerings. Shift is next, leveraging bilateral sound and music to meet people with approachable, trusted, and deeply human support that leaves them feeling better than when they came.”

7 Days of Shift – a 7-day guided program narrated by Calm meditation teacher Rose Nisker, pairing a few minutes of grounding wisdom with a bilateral track each day.

Shift Your State – 4 new bilateral tracks paired with looping visuals, each composed to shift people into one of four goal states: Focus, Release, Uplift, and Sleep.

Shift Music – an expanded library of new bilateral audio tracks for users to explore any time.

Among the new music is an exclusive bilateral remix of “The Record Player Song” from Daisy the Great. Originally released in 2018, the song became a breakout hit for the duo and has amassed more than 200 million streams across two versions. More recently, Daisy the Great reimagined the track using hocketing, a musical technique in which a single melody is split between two or more voices or instruments, alternating notes and rests, and the new version has gained massive traction across TikTok. It's the first of multiple tracks Calm and Daisy the Great will create together for Shift, continuing Calm’s long-standing approach of partnering with artists to create content that resonates with people.

“We started to make a lot of videos online singing with a technique called hocketing where we split up the melody line and pass it back-and-forth, and it makes a really awesome vocal effect. We did it with our song ‘The Record Player Song,’ and that one really seemed to resonate," said Daisy the Great. "That song already has a bit of a built-in bilateral quality with the melody passing between us, and the overlapping vocals, so it made a lot of sense for Shift. We're so, so excited to be working with Calm and their production team to not only share our music in a new way, but hopefully to help people feel good and connected to themselves too.”

Calm also collaborated with outside consultants certified by the EMDR International Association throughout Shift's development to ensure the content is credible, safe, and suitable for everyday, self-guided use.

“With Shift, Calm takes its already impressive collection of self-soothing programs to another level, thoughtfully integrating guided imagery, relaxing music, and gentle bilateral stimulation,” said Roy Kiessling, LISW. “As an experienced EMDR clinician and trainer, I appreciate the care Calm has taken to emphasize relaxation, emotional comfort, and positive resource enhancement. Shift offers a welcome, accessible way to incorporate soothing bilateral stimulation into everyday emotional well-being.”

Calm is a leading mental wellness company on a mission to make the world happier and healthier. Known for its flagship consumer app, ranked #1 in its category with over 180 million downloads and available in 10 languages across nearly 190 countries, Calm helps people sleep better, find stress relief, and live more mindfully through content and resources from experts and beloved celebrity voices. Building on this foundation, Calm has created a broader portfolio including Calm Health, a digital mental health solution offered through employers, health plans and providers to expand access to mental health and sleep support, boost benefits engagement, and drive positive health outcomes. Today, Calm supports more than 100K organizations and reaches over 42 million covered lives through Calm Health. Calm has been recognized as a TIME100 Most Influential Company and one of Fast Company’s Brands That Matter. Learn more at calm.com.

Daisy the Great is a New York duo made up of Mina Walker and Kelley Dugan, whose sharp, playful songwriting pairs tight harmonies with an uncanny melodic sensibility. The two met as acting majors at NYU and began writing together, turning their stacked harmonies and strange melodies into Daisy the Great. Their “Record Player Song” blew up on TikTok, and a version with AJR went gold with over 450 million streams. Their third album, The Rubber Teeth Talk, explores self-perception, insecurity, fear, and self-trust. They recently released The Rubber Teeth Talk With Friends, reimagining each song with a different artist offering an entirely new take and arrangement.
